Consider a hypothesis for a two-class problem. A set of N points or instances can be labeled as + or - in 2N ways. If for every such labeling, a function can be determined in ℋ.

A set S of examples is shattered by a set of functions H if for every partition of the examples in S into positive and negative examples, there is a function in H that gives exactly these labels to the examples.

Example 1: Hypothesis class of left-bounded intervals on the real axis [0, a) for some real number a > 0 (Fig. 5.6).

Figure 5.6  Positive region and negative region

Case 1: Let us assume that we have a set S with only one point (Fig. 5.7).

Figure 5.7  Set S with only one point

If the point is labeled +ve, then we can find a point a that is to the right of that point. Such hypothesis correctly labels the point as +ve.

If the point is labeled -ve, then we can find a point a that is to the left of that point. Such hypothesis correctly labels the point as -ve.

Thus, any set of one point can be shattered.

Case 2: Let us assume that we have a set S with two points (Fig. 5.8).

Figure 5.8  Points with incorrect labeling

We can label the points such that no hypothesis in this class matches the labels.

Example 2: Hypothesis class is a set of intervals on the real axis [a, b] for some real number b> a. Points within the range [a, b] are labelled +ve and outside the range as -ve.

Case 1: Let us assume that we have a set S with only one point (Fig. 5.9).

Figure 5.9  A set S with only one point

If the point is labelled +ve, then we can find two points a and b such that a is to the left of the point and b is to the right of the point. Such hypothesis correctly labels the point as +ve (Fig. 5.10).

Figure 5.10  A positive point between a and b

If the point is labeled -ve, then we can find two points a and b that are to the right or left of that point. Such hypothesis correctly labels the point as -ve. Thus, any set of one point can be shattered.

Case 2: Let us assume that we have a set S with two points (Fig. 5.11).

Figure 5.11  Set S with two points

Thus, any set of two points can be shattered.

Case 3: Let us assume that we have a set S with three points (Fig. 5.12).

Figure 5.12  Set S with three points

The set of three points cannot be shattered.

The VC dimension of hypothesis space H over instance space X is the size of the largest finite subset of X that is shattered by H.

If there exists any subset of size d that can be shattered, then VC(H) >  = d.

If no subset of size d can be shattered, then VC(H) < d.

For infinite hypothesis spaces, its VC dimension behaves like log(|H|).

The VC dimension quantifies the ability of a classifier in understanding complex patterns of data. The VC dimension of a classifier and its capacity to shatter sets of points are closely correlated. The larger the VC dimension of a classifier, the higher the capacity to shatter complicated sets of points. If the VC dimension of a classifier is low, the classifier struggles to understand the complex patterns of data and this results in overfitting or underfitting of data.

Using VC (H) as a measure, we can define Occam’s theorem for infinite hypothesis spaces. Given a sample D with m examples, find some h ϵ H which is consistent with m examples where

$m > \frac{1}{\varepsilon}\left( {8VC\left( H \right)\log\frac{13}{\varepsilon} + 4\log\frac{2}{\delta}} \right)$

Then, with a probability of 1- δ, the hypothesis space has error less than ε

5.13Worst Case (Online) Learning

Forecasting is not a one-time process but must be repeated again and again. Forecasts must be updated for the new data and decision-making must be automated in view of the new data. The ideal solution is to choose a procedure that is fully automated. The process must be robust as well. Online learning methods constitute a class of algorithms for making a sequence of repeated forecast decisions.

Online learning in ML refers to a paradigm where the algorithm learns sequentially from a stream of data, updating its model incrementally as new observations become available. While online learning offers advantages like adaptability to changing data and resource efficiency, several worst-case scenarios can impact its effectiveness:

•Concept drift: If the underlying patterns in the data change significantly over time, the model may struggle to adapt quickly. This leads to the degradation of the performance of the model.

•Catastrophic forgetting: When the model updates itself with new data, it might forget previously learned patterns, especially if the new data conflicts with earlier observations.

•Noisy data: Online learning models can be sensitive to noisy or erroneous data. If the incoming data contains a high level of noise, it can lead to incorrect model updates.

•Bias or imbalance: If the incoming data is biased or imbalanced, the model may become skewed towards certain patterns and struggle to learn from less represented data points.

•Adversarial attacks: Online learning systems might be vulnerable to adversarial attacks, where maliciously crafted data points can mislead the model’s learning process.

Online learning may struggle with computational constraints or limited memory, especially when dealing with vast amounts of streaming data. More complex models might require extensive computational resources for updating with each new data point, making them impractical for real-time learning.

To address these challenges, different strategies should be employed like feature engineering, robust model architectures, regularization techniques, and continuous monitoring for model performance and data quality.

•Regularization techniques: Regularization methods like L1/L2 regularization, dropout, or early stopping can prevent overfitting and help the model generalize better, even in the presence of noisy or changing data:

●L1 regularization (LASSO): Adds a penalty term proportional to the absolute value of the coefficients’ sum to the loss function.

●L2 regularization (Ridge): Adds a penalty term proportional to the square of the coefficients’ sum to the loss function. It penalizes large coefficients but does not usually force them to zero, smoothing out the impact on the model and reducing the magnitudes of the coefficients.

●Elastic net: Combines L1 and L2 regularization by adding both penalties to the loss function. This method helps overcome the limitations of L1 and L2 regularization by providing a balance between feature selection (L1) and coefficient shrinkage (L2).

•Ensemble methods: Employing ensemble methods, such as bagging or boosting, can improve model performance by combining multiple models, reducing variance, and making the system more resistant to noisy data or overfitting.

•Concept drift detection: Implement algorithms to detect concept drift early. Techniques like monitoring statistical measures or using drift-detection algorithms can help in identification when the data distribution shifts, allowing for timely model updates.

•Online feature selection: Feature selection techniques like information gain or recursive feature elimination can help in this regard.

•Robust training: Use robust optimization methods that are less sensitive to noise or outliers in the data. Techniques like robust regression or robust PCA can help mitigate the impact of noisy observations.

•Balancing data: Address imbalances in the data by employing techniques such as oversampling, undersampling, or synthetic data generation to ensure the model learns from all classes equally.

•Regularly monitor model performance and data quality, and update the model incrementally to adapt to changes in the data distribution.

•Resource optimization: Optimize computational resources by using incremental learning techniques, model compression, etc. without compromising performance.

By combining these approaches and continuously improving the model’s adaptability and resilience, it can become more capable of handling worst-case scenarios in online ML environments.

5.14Applications of Computational Learning Theory

The applications of CLT in ML are vast and varied. It is used to develop algorithms for supervised learning, unsupervised learning, reinforcement learning, and deep learning. It is also used to develop models for classification, clustering, and regression. In addition, computational learning theory is used to develop algorithms for feature selection, feature extraction, and model selection.

5.14.1Applications in Natural Language Processing

Machine translation is the process of automatically translating text from one language to another. CLT has been used to develop algorithms that can learn from large data sets of translated text to improve the accuracy of machine translation. These algorithms can learn from the patterns in the data, such as the syntax and grammar of the language, to better understand the meaning of the text and produce more accurate translations.

Text classification is the process of automatically assigning labels to text documents. CLT has been used to develop algorithms that can learn from labeled data to accurately classify text documents. These algorithms can learn from the patterns in the data, such as the words and phrases used in the text, to better understand the meaning of the text and assign the correct label.

Sentiment analysis is the process of automatically determining the sentiment or opinion expressed in text. CLT has been used to develop algorithms that can learn from labeled data to accurately identify the sentiment expressed in text. These algorithms can learn from the patterns in the data, such as the words and phrases used in the text, to better understand the sentiment expressed in the text.

In conclusion, CLT has become an important tool in NLP due to its ability to provide insights into the structure and meaning of language. As the field of NLP continues to evolve, computational learning theory will continue to play an important role in the development of new algorithms and applications.

5.14.2Applications in Computer Vision

Computer vision is the field of study that focuses on the development of algorithms that can interpret and understand visual data. It is used in a variety of applications, such as facial recognition, object recognition, and image segmentation. In order to achieve these tasks, computer vision algorithms must be able to learn from data and make predictions. This is where computational learning theory comes into play.

For example, a computer vision algorithm can be developed using CLT to recognize objects in an image. The algorithm can learn from the data and make predictions about what objects are in the image. Image segmentation is the process of dividing an image into multiple regions based on certain characteristics. This can be used to identify objects in an image or to separate foreground from background. Facial recognition is an important application of computer vision, as it can be used for security purposes or for identifying individuals. CLT can be used to develop algorithms that can learn from data and make predictions about facial features.

5.14.3Applications in Robotics

Robotics is a field of engineering that focuses on the design and development of robots. Robots are machines that are designed to perform tasks autonomously or semi-autonomously. As robots become more advanced, they are increasingly being used in a variety of applications, such as manufacturing, healthcare, and home automation.

CLT can be used to improve the performance of robotic systems. By applying CLT, robots can learn from their environment and adapt to changing conditions. This can be used to improve the accuracy and speed of the robot’s movements, as well as its ability to recognize objects and navigate its environment.

CLT can also be used to improve the safety of robotic systems. By applying CLT, robots can learn to detect and avoid obstacles, as well as recognize and respond to dangerous situations. This can help to reduce the risk of accidents and improve the safety of robotic systems.

Finally, CLT can be used to improve the efficiency of robotic systems. By applying CLT, robots can learn to recognize patterns and optimize their movements to save energy and time. This can help to reduce the cost of operating robotic systems and improve their overall efficiency.

In conclusion, CLT can be used to improve the performance, safety, and efficiency of robotic systems. As robots become more advanced, CLT will continue to be an important tool for improving the performance of robotic systems.

5.15Evaluation Metrics for Computational Learning Theory

Evaluation metrics for CLT are important for assessing the accuracy and performance of ML algorithms. Evaluation metrics provide a quantitative measure of how well an ML algorithm performs on a given task. This is important for understanding the strengths and weaknesses of different algorithms and for choosing the best algorithm for a particular application.

Accuracy is one of the most-used evaluation metrics for ML algorithms. It is calculated by dividing the number of correctly classified data points by the total number of data points. Accuracy is a good measure of performance when the classes are balanced, but it can be misleading when the classes are imbalanced.

Precision and recall are two other important evaluation metrics for ML algorithms. Precision is a measure of how many of the predicted positive results are actually correct. It is calculated by dividing the number of true positives by the total number of predicted positives. Recall is a measure of how many of the actual positive results were correctly predicted. It is calculated by dividing the number of true positives by the total number of actual positives.

F-measure is a combination of precision and recall. It is calculated by taking the harmonic mean of precision and recall. The F-measure is a good metric for evaluating ML algorithms when the classes are imbalanced.

AUC-ROC (area under the curve-receiver operating characteristic) is a metric used to evaluate the performance of binary classifiers. It is calculated by plotting the true positive rate against the false positive rate.

5.16Future Directions in Computational Learning Theory

CLT is a field of study that focuses on the development of algorithms and techniques that can be used to learn from data. It has become increasingly important in recent years, as the amount of data available to us has grown exponentially.

One of the most promising areas of research is the development of deep learning algorithms. These algorithms can learn from large amounts of data and can be used to solve complex problems. These algorithms are based on ANNs, which are modeled on the structure of the human brain. By using deep learning algorithms, machines can learn to recognize patterns in data and make predictions about future outcomes.

Another potential direction is the development of reinforcement learning algorithms. These algorithms are based on the idea of reward and punishment and can be used to teach machines to perform certain tasks. Finally, another direction for CLT is the development of transfer learning algorithms, which are based on the idea of transferring knowledge from one domain to another.

All these directions could be used to improve the accuracy of ML algorithms and to make them more efficient.

5.16.1Advances in Deep Learning Related to Computational Learning Theory

Deep learning is a rapidly advancing field of AI that has seen tremendous growth in recent years. It is based on the idea of using ANNs to mimic the way the human brain works. Deep learning has been used to solve a wide range of problems, from image recognition to NLP. In particular, advances in deep learning have had a significant impact on CLT.

One of the most important advances in deep learning related to computational learning theory is the development of convolutional neural networks (CNNs). CNNs are a type of neural network that are specifically designed to recognize patterns in images. They are composed of layers of neurons that are connected to each other in a way that allows them to recognize patterns in images. They have been used to solve a variety of problems, such as object recognition, facial recognition, and image segmentation.

Another important advance is the development of recurrent neural networks (RNNs). RNNs are a type of neural network that are specifically designed to process sequences of data. They are composed of layers of neurons that are connected to each other in a way that allows them to process sequences.

5.16.2Explainable AI Related to Computational Learning Theory

Explainable AI (XAI) is a branch of AI that focuses on making AI systems more transparent and interpretable. It is closely related to CLT. CLT is concerned with understanding the mathematical principles underlying the design and analysis of learning algorithms, while XAI is concerned with understanding how these algorithms can be used to explain the behavior of AI systems.

The goal of XAI is to make AI systems more transparent and interpretable so that humans can better understand and trust them. This is important because AI systems are increasingly being used to make decisions that have a significant impact on people’s lives, such as in healthcare, finance, and criminal justice.

5.16.3Quantum Machine Learning Related to Computational Learning Theory

Quantum machine learning (QML) is a rapidly growing field of research that combines the power of quantum computing with ML algorithms to create powerful new ways of solving complex problems. QML has the potential to revolutionize the way we think about ML and CLT.

Quantum computing is based on the principles of quantum mechanics, which allow for the manipulation of information at a much faster rate than traditional computing. This enables the development of algorithms that can solve complex problems in a fraction of the time. By combining quantum computing with ML algorithms, QML can be used to solve problems that are too complex for traditional computing.

The advantages of using quantum computing include the ability to process large amounts of data quickly, the ability to solve problems that are too complex for traditional computing, and the ability to use quantum entanglement to solve problems faster. In addition, quantum computing can be used to create algorithms that can learn from data and adapt to changing conditions.

The challenges associated with quantum computing include the difficulty of creating algorithms that are accurate and reliable, the need for specialized hardware, and the difficulty of scaling up quantum computing systems. In addition, quantum computing is still in its infancy and there is much to be learned about the technology.

The potential applications of QML are vast. QML can be used to create algorithms that can analyze large data sets, identify patterns in data, and make predictions. QML can also be used to create algorithms that can identify and classify objects, detect anomalies in data, and create models that can be used to make decisions. Thus, QML is a rapidly growing field of research that has the potential to revolutionize CLT.

Summary

•Computational learning theory is a branch of artificial intelligence that focuses on the design and analysis of algorithms that learn from data. It is a relatively new field of research, but it has already had a significant impact on the development of machine learning and artificial intelligence.

•The main objective (goal) is to develop algorithms that can learn from data and make predictions about future data. Another objective (goal) is to understand the boundaries (limits) of what can be learned from data. This includes being aware of the learning algorithms’ sample complexity.

•The main methods used in computational learning theory are inductive learning, deductive learning, abductive learning, and reinforcement learning.

•The complexity of a learning algorithm refers to the amount of time and resources required to produce a model.

•The computational complexity of a learning algorithm is determined by the number of operations it requires to produce a model.

•Mistake-bound learning is a model that tries to capture the essence of how humans learn from their mistakes.

•Instance-based learning, also known as exemplar-based learning, is a form of ML in which the model learns by storing and classifying individual examples, as opposed to following predefined rules.

•Eager learning is a type of learning where the system learns a model from the training data before any queries are made. This is also known as model-based learning.

•Generative learning is an ML approach that entails constructing a model that represents the process by which the data is generated.

•CLT has been applied to a variety of fields, including robotics.

•Explainable AI (XAI) is a branch of AI that focuses on making AI systems more transparent and interpretable.

•Quantum machine learning (QML) is a rapidly growing field of research that combines the power of quantum computing with machine learning algorithms to create powerful new ways of solving complex problems.

6

Machine Learning Models

Learning Objectives

At the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

•Explain the different types of machine learning models, including logical, geometric, distance, and probabilistic

•Identify and work with various types of features

•Perform statistical operations on features

•Apply feature transformation techniques, including feature scaling and normalization

•Implement feature selection and feature learning methods

•Explain concept learning in detail

6.1Introduction

In the previous chapter, we discussed computational learning theory (CLT), which is a branch of ­theoretical computer science that studies the design and analysis of machine learning (ML) models and algorithms. ML models are mathematical representations of data and patterns that can be used for prediction, ­classification, clustering, etc. They are procedures that can learn from data and optimize the parameters of ML models. One way to understand the relationships between CLT, ML models and ML algorithms is to use a table that compares them along different dimensions, such as is shown in Table 6.1.

Table 6.1Differences between CLT, ML algorithms and ML models

Dimension

CLT

ML algorithm

ML model

Goal

To provide theoretical ­guarantees and bounds on the performance and ­complexity of ML methods.

To find the optimal or near-optimal parameters of ML models that minimize a loss function or maximize a utility function.

To capture the underlying structure and regularities of data and make predictions or decisions based on them.

Example

PAC learning, VC ­dimension, Rademacher complexity, etc.

Gradient descent, ­stochastic gradient descent, ­expectation maximization, K-means, etc.

Linear regression, logistic regression, neural networks, decision trees, etc.

Challenge

To deal with the trade-off between expressiveness and generalization, and to cope with the uncertainty and noise in data.

To find efficient and ­scalable algorithms that can converge to good solutions in high-dimensional and large-scale problems.

To choose the appropriate model complexity and avoid overfitting or underfitting of data.

6.2Models in Machine Learning

The data used for ML usually consists of attributes and labels. Attributes are the features or variables that describe the data, such as height, weight, color. Labels are the outcomes or targets we want to predict or explain, such as class, category, score. Each combination of attributes and labels is called an instance, representing a single observation or example in the data.

For example, if we want to predict whether a person has diabetes or not based on their blood pressure and glucose level, each person’s blood pressure and glucose level are the attributes and their diabetes status is the label.

The instance space is the set of all possible instances generated from the attributes. The outcome space is the set of all possible labels that can be assigned to the instances. For example, if we have two attributes, blood pressure and glucose level, each with 10 possible values, the instance space has 10 × 10 = 100 possible instances. If we have two possible labels, diabetes or no diabetes, the outcome space has two possible outcomes. Sometimes, the instance and outcome spaces are the same, such as when we want to cluster the instances into groups based on their similarity.

An ML model mathematically represents the relationship between the qualities and the label. It can be seen as a function that maps an instance to an outcome. The model can be learned from the data using various algorithms and techniques.

Broadly, ML models are classified into three categories: logical, geometrical, and probabilistic.

6.2.1Logical Models

Logical models are ML models that use rules or conditions to make predictions or classifications. They are also known as rule-based or tree models because they often have a tree-like structure, where each node represents a rule or a condition and each branch represents an outcome or a decision. Logical models are easy to interpret and explain because they can be translated into natural language statements that follow if-then logic.

Consider the data plotted to predict the type of breast cancer shown in Fig. 6.1.

This plot shows a clear separation between malignant and benign cases based on age and tumor size. Given their age and tumor size, we can use this information to create a logical model that can predict the cancer type for a new patient. One possible rule for such a logical model could be:

if age> a1 and tumour size> t1, then malignant, else benign

Figure 6.1  Data plot between age and tumor size

This is a simple example of a rule-based model or a tree model, where the condition (age > a1 and tumor size > t1) is the root node, and the outcomes (malignant or benign) are the leaf nodes. The condition can be further split into two sub-conditions (age > a1 and tumour size > t1), which form the internal nodes of the tree.

Consider the data shown in Table 6.2. It consists of five attributes, of which four are feature attributes and one is an outcome attribute. There are 14 data instances, and the outcome attribute is Play_Tennis, which takes either yes or no values. A logical tree model can be built based on this data. The tree thus formed is called a decision tree (Fig. 6.2). The most popular decision tree algorithms are iterative dichotomizer 3.0 (ID3) and classification and regression trees (CART).

6.2.2Geometrical Models

Here, the data is represented in a 2D or 3D hyperplane. Data with four or more attributes is difficult to visualize and can only be imagined in a virtual space. Geometric models are helpful in ML because they make it possible to see the connection between a data set’s input attributes and output labels. We can observe how the data is distributed and clustered based on its class label by showing each data instance as a point in a hyperplane. This can assist us in selecting the best ML algorithm to analyze the data and generate precise predictions.

Linear models are geometrical models with linearly separable outcome space. Consider simple data with two attributes and one outcome. Assume that the number of unique outcomes is two. This is called a two-class problem. Each instance can be represented in a two-dimensional plane as a point. The point is represented based on the class label.

For example, consider the simple logical AND data shown in Table 6.3. The visual representation of the data is shown in Fig. 6.3. Here, each data tuple is shown as a point in the 2D plane depicting the class label. The points with label 0 are represented as circles, and those with label 1 are represented as squares. After plotting the data over a plane, the data is linearly separable if a straight line separates the data points. Otherwise, it is linearly inseparable.

The weights are the model parameters whose values are determined during training. Logistic regression and multilayer perceptron are a few examples of linear models.

If, however, the data cannot be separated linearly, we may need to categorize it using a non-linear model, such as a neural network or decision tree. A non-linear model looks for a non-linear boundary (such as a curve or a complicated form) that divides the data points into several classes, rather than assuming a linear relationship between the input features and the output labels.

Consider the XOR problem. Here, the data has only two dimensions, but it is linearly inseparable. Real-time data may only sometimes be linear and it usually has more attributes. Such data need not be linearly separable. Kernel methods can be employed to check whether the data in higher dimensional space is linearly separable.

Therefore, by using geometric models, we can gain insight into the nature of the data and select an appropriate ML algorithm for our problem.

6.2.2.1Distance Models

Distance models are a type of geometrical model that use a distance metric to separate the outcome spaces. The distance metric determines how far away two points are in a particular space. The Manhattan distance metric, for instance, calculates the total of the absolute differences between two points’ coordinates, while the Euclidean distance metric calculates the straight line distance between two places.

Data is plotted over a 2D plane or a 3D hyperplane, depending on the number of features or dimensions. A 2D plane has two features, height, and weight, while a 3D hyperplane has three features: length, width, and depth. The goal is to find a way to separate the different groups of data based on their distances.

One way to do this is to calculate the centroid of each data group. The centroid is the average of all the points in a group. It represents the center of mass or gravity of the group. Calculating the distance between two groups of centroids allows one to determine how far apart they are. The groups are increasingly similar the smaller the distance between them. They differ more sharply the further apart they are.

Distance-based geometrical models can be used for clustering or classification tasks. Distance-based geometrical models are useful in ML because they can help us discover patterns and structures in data and reduce the dimensionality and complexity of data. They can also help us measure the similarity or dissimilarity between data points, which can help find outliers, anomalies, or similarities. These distances are defined in equations.

Consider that there are n points plotted over a 2D x-y plane.

Euclidean distance: $\sqrt{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( {x_{i} - y_{i}} \right)^{2}}$

Manhattan distance: $\sqrt{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left| {x_{i} - y_{i}} \right|}$

Minkowski distance: $\left( {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left| {x_{i} - y_{i}} \right|^{p}} \right)^{1/p}$

Minkowski distance is the general distance metric. By substituting p = 1, we get the Manhattan distance. If we substitute p = 2, we get the Euclidean distance.

6.2.3Probabilistic Models

Probabilistic models are a class of models that incorporate uncertainty and randomness in their structure and predictions. They are widely used in ML to capture the variability and complexity of real-world data. Probabilistic models can be divided into two categories: predictive and generative.

Predictive models estimate the conditional probability of an outcome, given some input attributes. For example, a predictive model can answer questions like “What is the probability of a customer buying a product given their age, gender, and browsing history?” or “What is the probability of a patient having a disease given their symptoms and test results?” Predictive models are often used for classification and regression tasks, where the goal is to assign a label or a value to an input instance.

Generative models estimate the joint probability of both the input and the outcome attributes. For example, a generative model can answer questions like “What is the probability of observing a customer with a certain age, gender, and browsing history buying a certain product?” or “What is the probability of observing a patient with certain symptoms and test results having a certain disease?” Generative models are often used for unsupervised learning tasks, where the goal is to discover the underlying structure and patterns of the data.

One of the advantages of probabilistic models is that they can provide point estimates, confidence intervals, and error bounds for their predictions. This can help quantify the uncertainty and reliability of the model’s outputs. Another advantage is that they can incorporate prior knowledge and beliefs into the model’s parameters using Bayesian inference. This can help improve the model’s performance and robustness, especially when the data is scarce or noisy.

Some examples of probabilistic models in ML are:

•Naive Bayes: A simple and efficient predictive model that assumes conditional independence among the input attributes given the outcome. It uses Bayes’ theorem to compute the posterior probability of each outcome given the input attributes.

•Logistic Regression: A predictive model that uses a logistic function to simulate the likelihood of a binary result, given a set of input characteristics. It might be considered a specific instance of a generalized linear model.

•Gaussian Mixture Model: A generative model that assumes that a combination of Gaussian distributions with unidentified parameters produces data. It assigns each data point to a cluster and estimates the mixture model’s parameters using the expectation maximization approach.

•Hidden Markov Model: A generative model that assumes data is generated from a Markov chain with hidden states. It uses dynamic programming algorithms such as the forward-backward algorithm and the Viterbi algorithm to infer the hidden states and estimate the parameters of the Markov chain.

Let X represent the feature values and Y the value of the outcome. The probabilistic model establishes the relationship between X and Y using conditional or joint probability.

P(Y | X ) represents conditional probability and is read as ‘the probability of Y given X,’ that is, determining the probability of the outcome, given the feature values. It is determined using Bayes’ theorem.

$P\left( {Y\text{|}X} \right) = \frac{P\left( {X\text{|}Y} \right)P\left( Y \right)}{P\left( X \right)}$

It is read descriptively as

$\text{Posterior} = \frac{\text{Likelihood*Prior}}{\text{Evidence}}$

P(Y , X ) represents joint probability. It is defined as

P (Y , X ) = P(Y ∩ X ) = P (X|Y )* P (Y) = P (Y |X )* P (X)

The concept of joint probability is used to generate the data points. These probabilistic models are discussed in detail in Chapter 7.

6.3Features

A feature is a measurement that is mapped to the outcome. Mathematically, a feature can be defined as a function that maps an instance space of an attribute to possible values for the attribute. All possible values for an attribute constitute the domain of the feature space. Features are categorized based on their domain space. Certain features are real numbers or integers, whereas some are discrete values.

Features are inputs fed into an ML model to learn a function that can produce the desired output. For instance, to create a model that can categorize photographs of dogs and cats, we must first take elements from the images that would aid the model in differentiating between the two classes. These features could be the color, shape, size, texture, or any other property of the image that is relevant to the task. The quality and quantity of features affect the performance of the model. The best features are those that capture the most information and variation in the data while reducing noise and redundancy.

6.3.1Types of Features

Based on their values, features are roughly categorized as follows:

•Numerical characteristics: These characteristics have discrete or continuous numerical values. Interval and ratio features are subcategories of numerical features. Interval features lack an absolute zero point but have a significant value differential between them (for instance, the temperature in Celsius or Fahrenheit). The absolute zero point and a considerable difference are present in ratio features (for example, height, weight, or wealth).

•Categorical characteristics: These characteristics have defined values that fall into groups. Nominal and ordinal features are the subcategories. Nominal characteristics are those that lack a natural hierarchy among the categories (for instance, nationality or hair color). Ordinal characteristics are those that fall into a certain hierarchy or order (for example, customer happiness or educational level). Data can be grouped, counted, or compared using categorical attributes.

•Binary features: These are a specific kind of categorical feature that can have two possible values. For example, marital status, gender, and the existence of illness. Logical operations or categorization can both use binary characteristics.

•Temporal features: These are characteristics that symbolize temporal attributes such as date, time, duration and frequency. Data trends, patterns, cycles, or seasonality can all be determined by temporal properties.

•Text features: These serve as a representation of text data. Text features include product reviews, tweets, news stories, etc. Natural language processing (NLP) tasks like sentiment analysis, topic modeling and text summarization can use text features.

6.3.2Statistical Operations on Features

Along with the feature space’s domain, other important aspects include the kinds of operations that can be carried out on features. Take the two elements employee_id and employee_salary. Integers make up the features’ domain space. It makes sense to use statistical procedures like mean on the employee_salary variable. However, statistical procedures like mean and median have no significance on employee_id.

The significant operations that can be carried out come under three main groups:

•Measures of Central Tendency: Used to give a single value to the entirety of the data.

•Scattering Statistics: This determines how far the data deviates from the mean. It is applied to understand data dispersion.

•Shape Measures: These characterize how the data is distributed or arranged within a data set.

Mean, median, and mode are the three primary operations that fall under measurements of central tendency. The mean shows the average value. When all the values are placed in ascending order, the median reflects the middle value. The mode shows the highest frequency value. While mode can be applied to any domain, mean and median can only feature values with integer or real number domain spaces.

Data dispersion is frequently understood using variance and standard deviation. Percentiles are another way to assess dispersion. Quartiles are typically used to quantify dispersion. When quartiles are multiplied by 25, they are referred to as percentiles. To understand the form of the data distribution, histograms and cumulative distribution plots are utilized.

We may think about the following aspects to clarify these claims with examples and show how it aids in ML:

•Statistical procedures on features enable meaningful summarization, analysis, and visualization of the data. They also assist us in locating data abnormalities such as outliers, missing values, skewness, and other irregularities that might impair the effectiveness of ML models.

•For instance, we can utilize mean, median, and mode to identify the central tendency of the wage feature and anticipate an employee’s salary based on their experience, education, and talents. This can help us understand the data set’s median, typical, or average salary. We can also use variance and standard deviation to determine how much the wage deviates from the mean or how it is distributed. This can aid in our comprehension of the scope and range of the salary feature. The salary feature can also be divided into four equal groups based on values using quartiles or percentiles. This enables us to evaluate various wage feature subsets and spot outliers or extreme values that might impact the forecast.

•Similarly, we may use histograms and cumulative distribution plots to analyze the shape distribution of data like word count, punctuation marks, capital letters, etc., if we want to identify an email as spam or not based on its content. These plots can show how values are distributed across the range of values and how frequently or infrequently they appear in the features. This can assist us in spotting patterns or trends in the characteristics of emails that indicate whether they are spam or not.

•Before using any ML algorithm, studying and comprehending the data is essential. Therefore, statistical operations on features are helpful in this regard. They also assist us in preprocessing the data, such as scaling, normalizing, encoding, etc., to make it appropriate for ML models. They also help us compare and evaluate various ML models based on their performance characteristics, such as recall, accuracy, and precision.

6.3.3Feature Transformation

Changing the domain of a data set’s features is known as feature transformation. This has many applications:

•Improving the data’s suitability for an ML model. For instance, certain models call for a specific normalization, standardization, or data encoding.

•Making the data less complex or multidimensional. As an illustration, certain elements could be unnecessary, unimportant, or noisy and might be eliminated or blended with other aspects.

•Enhancing the model’s functionality or interpretability. One way to better capture this relationship is to convert certain features that, for instance, may have a non-linear relationship with the target variable.

•Visualizing the distribution or organization of the data. For instance, some features with a high degree of dimension can be projected onto a space with a lower degree of dimension using techniques like principal component analysis (PCA) or t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE).

Scaling of features, which modifies the range or size of the features, is a typical feature modification. This is frequently required when the characteristics have varied units or magnitudes and might impact how some models learn. Consider a data set of employees where the two features are age and income. Age may be between 25 and 100 years, and income may be between 25000 and 250000 INR. The income factor will predominate the clustering results if such data is input to a model like K-means clustering, which uses distance-based metrics and has a considerably more significant scale than age. To avoid this, feature scaling can be utilized to scale the features similarly.

As it can increase the quality and usefulness of the data and eventually improve the model’s performance and interpretability, feature transformation is a crucial stage in ML.

6.3.3.1Feature Scaling or Normalization

MinMax scaling is a straightforward method that data scientists frequently use. This scaler function transforms the data into the range [0, 1]. As a result, the original data’s minimum value becomes 0 and its highest value becomes 1. The remaining values are correspondingly scaled between 0 and 1. For instance, if the original data contained values between 10 and 100, applying MinMax scaling would produce values between 0 and 1, where 10 would become 0, 100 would become 1, and 50 would become 0.5.

In ML, MinMax scaling is helpful because it can assist in normalizing the data and lessen the impact of outliers. Some ML techniques, such as gradient descent and K-means clustering, can perform and converge better with normalized data. In contrast to other scaling techniques that could alter the original data, MinMax scaling can also aid in maintaining the shape and distribution of the data.

The MinMax scaler is defined as follows:

(6.1)

$\frac{x - x_{min}}{x_{max} - x_{min}}$

When we use Equation (6.1) on the data given in Table 6.5, the scaled data is normalized, as is shown in Table 6.6.

Standard Scaling: ML obtains many benefits from standard scaling. Removing each feature’s units and scale first makes the data more comparable. For instance, if we have two features, one measured in meters and the other in kilometers, standard scaling would make the features dimensionless and on the same scale. Scaling the data by variation and centering it around zero also lessens the impact of outliers. For instance, standard scaling may make extreme values that are significantly larger or smaller than the rest of a feature closer to the mean and less significant. Thirdly, it enhances the performance of some ML methods that depend on the magnitude of the features or presumes that the data is regularly distributed. For instance, when the data is standardized, gradient descent, which is used to optimize numerous models, converges more quickly.

Standard scaling is defined as follows:

(6.2)

$\frac{x - x_{\text{mean}}}{\text{Standard~deviation}}$

Standard deviation of age: The standard deviation is a measure of how much the data values vary from the mean. To calculate the standard deviation of the given data, we need to follow these steps:

1.Find the mean of the data by adding all the values and dividing by the number of values. In this case, the mean is (25 + 28 + 50 + 44) / 4 = 36.75.

2.Subtract the mean from each value and square the result. This gives us the squared deviations from the mean. For example, for the first value, we have (25 – 36.75)^2 = 138.0625.

3.Add up all the squared deviations and divide by the number of values. This gives us the variance of the data. In this case, the variance is (138.0625 + 76.5625 + 175.5625 + 52.5625) / 4 = 110.6875.

4.Take the square root of the variance to get the standard deviation. In this case, the standard deviation is sqrt(110.6875) = 10.52.

Therefore, the standard deviation of the age is 10.52.

Standard deviation of income:

1.Find the mean of the data by adding up all the values and dividing by the number of values. In this case, the mean is (18000 + 22000 + 65000 + 75000) / 4 = 45000.

2.Find the deviation of each value from the mean by subtracting the mean from each value. The deviations are –27000, –23000, 20000 and 30000.

3.Square each deviation to get rid of the negative signs and make the values more comparable. The squared deviations are 729000000, 529000000, 400000000 and 900000000.

4.Find the sum of the squared deviations by adding them up. The sum is 2558000000.

5.Divide the sum by the number of values to get the variance, which is a measure of how spread out the data is around the mean. The variance is 2558000000 / 4 = 639500000.

6.Take the square root of the variance to get the standard deviation, which is in the same units as the original data. The standard deviation is sqrt(639500000) = 25288.36.

Therefore, the standard deviation of the income data of 4 people is 25288.36.

6.3.3.2Other Transformation Techniques

Thresholding: Using a cut-off value, the thresholding approach turns a numerical or ordinal property into a binary feature. For instance, using thresholding, we may generate a new feature called age_group with only two values: 0 for young and 1 for elderly, given an existing feature called age a range of 0 to 100. To accomplish this, we must select a threshold number, such as 40, and assign the value 0 to all instances with age below 40 and the value 1 to all instances with age at or above 40. In this case, the cut-off point is 40, determined manually or by examining the age feature’s distribution.

Thresholding is helpful in ML for the following reasons:

•It can convert a continuous or ordinal characteristic into a categorical one to lower the dimensionality of the data. This may ease the handling and visualization of the data.

•It can produce more insightful features that better reflect some crucial facets of the data. For example, instead of using the precise blood pressure reading, thresholding may be used to generate a characteristic that shows whether or not a person has high blood pressure to forecast whether or not they have a particular disease.

•It can enhance the performance of various ML methods, including decision trees and logistic regression, which perform better with binary features.

Discretization: A quantitative feature value is converted to an ordinal feature value through discretization. A quantitative feature value, such as a person’s height, weight, or age, is a numerical number that can be any value within a range. A categorical value with a natural order, such as small, medium, or big, is an ordinal feature value. A quantitative feature’s range is discretized into intervals, giving each interval an ordinal value. Every interval is regarded as a bin with an associated ordinal value. The age feature, for instance, can be discretized into bins like [0–10], [11–20], [21–30], and so on, and each bin can be given an ordinal value like young, teen, adult, and so forth. This method is also known as binning.

ML can benefit from discretization for a number of reasons. Combining comparable values can first reduce the noise and outliers in the data. By limiting the range of possible values, it can make data computation and analysis simpler. Thirdly, employing meaningful categories rather than numbers can help make the data easier to read and comprehend. It can also enhance the performance of ML methods, such as decision trees or naive Bayes, that perform better with categorical information than numerical features.

There are many discretization techniques based on how the intervals are specified and how the ordinal values are assigned. Constant width discretization is a technique for dividing a feature’s range into intervals of equal width. For instance, if we wish to build 10 bins and the age range is [0–100], each bin will have a width of 10. Constant frequency discretization is a different technique that separates a feature’s range into intervals with a fixed number of instances. For instance, if we have 100 instances of age and want to divide them into 10 bins, each bin will have 10 occurrences. Although constant frequency discretization can prevent the creation of empty or sparse bins, it can also result in intervals of varying sizes.

6.3.4Feature Construction

Building new features from those already present in a data set is known as feature creation. When a data set comprises many features, but not all are equally significant or relevant for the ML task, feature creation can be helpful. In these circumstances, adding new features by combining those already present can make the feature vector more dimensional, which can result in overfitting or inefficient computation. To get around this issue, one can use feature selection techniques like a filter or wrapper approaches or dimensionality reduction techniques like principal component analysis (PCA) to reduce the number of features, while retaining the most useful ones.

Feature building can be used when a data set comprises categorical characteristics, but the ML model requires numerical inputs. For instance, variables like gender, color, or nationality cannot be used as direct inputs into a regression or neural network model if the data set contains those features. In these circumstances, feature encoding techniques like one-hot encoding, label encoding, or hashing can be used to transform the category characteristics into numerical values. However, these methods can also make the feature vector more dimensional and add sparsity or redundancy. As a result, one may also use feature creation techniques to transform existing categorical features into new numerical ones that capture more valuable data.

Applying arithmetic operations, such as addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division, to any existing feature is a quick approach to creating new features from the ones that already exist. Finding the Cartesian product of two distinct features, such as concatenating or multiplying them, and finding the ratio between two features, such as percentage or proportion, is a third method for creating new features.

6.3.5Feature Selection

Feature selection means choosing a subset of features from the initial feature set that are pertinent and instructive for the learning process. After feature creation, which generates new features from the raw data or existing features, feature selection is frequently carried out. While feature selection can help to lessen the redundancy and irrelevant features, feature creation can help to increase the quality and diversity of the feature set.

Depending on whether the target variable is present or not, feature selection can be applied to both supervised and unsupervised learning models. The target variable may be used as a criterion in feature selection in supervised learning to assess the utility of the features. Other criteria, such as clustering quality, information content, or statistical dependence, may be used for feature selection in unsupervised learning. The preprocessing step of feature selection is thought to provide various advantages for the learning task, including:

•Dimensionality reduction: Feature selection can reduce the dimensionality of the data by choosing a lower number of features, making the data simpler to visualize, comprehend, and manage.

•Decreased computational cost and training time: Feature selection, particularly for complicated models with several parameters and processes, can decrease training time by lowering the number of features.

•Reduction of overfitting: Feature selection can aid in preventing overfitting by removing redundant or irrelevant features. Overfitting occurs when the model learns too much from the noise or specific patterns in the training data and cannot generalize well to new or unknown data.

•Improvement of generalization: Choosing informative and representative features can assist the learning model in performing and performing accurately on new or unknown data, representing its ability to generalize well to many contexts and scenarios.

•Simplifying the structure and complexity of the learning model: By lowering the number of features, feature selection can help make the learning model simpler and easier to understand.

It is possible to execute feature selection in supervised learning using a variety of approaches, which can generally be divided into three categories: filtering, wrapper, and intrinsic methods.

Filtering method: This method ranks and assesses the features based on statistical or information-theoretic metrics, such as mutual information, chi-squared test and correlation, without using a learning model. The final subset is then chosen from the features with high scores. Filtering techniques are quick and scalable, but they must consider how the features interact or how well they work with the learning model.

The metrics used for filtering are information gain, Fisher’s score, chi-squared test, and so on. These metrics are used by considering each attribute and the labeled attribute. Information gain determines entropy reduction. Each feature attribute correlates with the labeled output and checks whether the two features correlate positively or negatively. The negatively correlated feature can be dropped accordingly. Fisher’s score ranks the attribute based on Fisher’s criteria. The features with large Fisher’s score can be considered and the other features can be discarded. A chi-squared test is used to find the relationship between each feature and the labeled feature.

Wrapper method: These methods assess the characteristics using a learning model as a black box. On a validation set or by utilizing cross-validation, they look for the ideal subset of features that maximizes a specific performance parameter, such as accuracy, precision, recall, etc. Compared to filtering methods, wrapper approaches are more precise and adaptable, but are also more computationally expensive and prone to overfitting. In wrapper methods, features are selected through a search mechanism over the feature space. The greedy method is used in wrapper methods for the feature selection process. It explores all possible combinations and selects the best features. The process will be initiated by selecting a subset of features and training the model using those features. The features can be added or subtracted depending on the output to improve the model’s performance. The popular algorithms used for feature selection in this category are forward selection, backward elimination, etc.

Intrinsic learning methods: During the training phase, these methods either alter the target function or employ regularization approaches to penalize or remove unnecessary or redundant characteristics. Although intrinsic approaches are effective and adaptive, they are model-specific and might not work with all learning models. Intrinsic methods can be considered a hybrid method that uses the advantages of both filter and wrapper methods. The feature selection process is also iterative and reduces computational costs. Features are selected such that each feature contributes to the model’s performance. The popular methods used in this category are LASSO regularization and random forest.

Forward selection is an iterative process. It starts with a single feature and iteratively adds features, and evaluates the model in each iteration. The process ends when a newly added feature does not improve the model’s performance. Backward elimination is the reverse of forward selection. This method considers all the features first, and then the model is evaluated. The process is repeated by removing the least significant feature in each iteration. The iterative process stops when there is no improvement in the model’s performance.

The data is plotted over a hyperplane and finds the best-fit line to determine the relationships among the data. This process is called data fitting. The model can choose the best-fit line by undergoing a learning process. Once a model is learned, it is subjected to evaluation. This helps us to understand whether the model is overfitted or underfitted.

The model can best fit the data when it finds all patterns or relationships in the data and ignores the random data points. A model is said to be overfitted if it covers all the data points and random points. A model is said to be underfitted if it does not find any relationship among the data points and cannot determine to which category the test data belongs.

Regularization means adjusting or tuning the ML model to minimize the loss function preventing overfitting or underfitting.

LASSO or L1 regularization: Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator, or LASSO, is used for regression methods. LASSO regularization modifies overfitted or underfitted models by adding a penalty term to the loss function. The penalty term is usually the sum of the absolute values of the coefficients used in the model. It is represented mathematically as follows:

(6.3)

Cost = Loss + λ + ∑w,

where λ represents the penalty term and w is the slope of the curve fit over the data.

The penalty term is calculated by adding the absolute values of the model’s coefficients. LASSO regularization shrinks the coefficients to zero and is also used for dimensionality reduction. It estimates the median of the data. LASSO regularization produces sparse models with few coefficients because other coefficients are shrunk to zero.

Ridge or L2 regularization: Here, the penalty term is the sum of the squares of the coefficients. It also shrinks the coefficients but is not set to zero. It is represented mathematically as

(6.4)

Cost = Loss + λ + ∑w2

6.4Concept Learning

Concept learning seeks to extract the definition of a broad category from the input data. For instance, concept learning can be trained to recognize which animal photos fall under the category of dogs, given a batch of animal images. The challenge of inferring a Boolean-valued function from the given data, where the function returns true for examples that belong to the idea and false for instances that do not, is another way to conceptualize learning. Thus, concept learning is the process of identifying the input feature–output label mapping that best matches the training data.

Depending on the nature and structure of the data, the complexity and expressiveness of the hypothesis space, and the selection criteria for the best hypothesis, various concepts can be learned differently. A set of potential functions that can be utilized to express the idea is known as a hypothesis space. The hypothesis space is the set of all feasible linear functions, for instance, if a linear combination of input features specifies the notion. Finding the function that minimizes a certain error or loss function on the training data is the objective of concept learning, which may be considered a search problem over the hypothesis space.

ML benefits from concept learning because it enables us to extrapolate from particular examples to novel and unforeseen situations. We can anticipate or categorize new data that we have not seen before by learning a concept from a small, noisy sample of data. Understanding the fundamental structure and logic of the concept can also help us find patterns and regularities in the data. Concept learning applies to many fields and applications, including bioinformatics, computer vision, speech recognition, and natural language processing.

While representing an instance as a hypothesis, each attribute has two more values (?,.ϕ) representing the most general and most specific hypothesis. Thus, the hypothesis space (ℋ) contains 5 × 4 × 4 × 4 × 4 × 4 = 5120 syntactically distinct hypotheses.
