Then, the network’s neurons are fed information about these traits. Each neuron in the network has a weight, like the weights your friend assigned to the attributes. The network integrates these weights with the input attributes to determine whether the fruit is an apple or an orange. The ANN changes these weights through a process known as training, using a set of model fruits you supply. First, it compares its forecast to the correct response (which you supply) to increase its accuracy over time. Then it modifies the weights accordingly. It does this repeatedly with more and more instances until it masters classifying these fruits. Once trained, the ANN will use the modified weights to determine if a new fruit it has not seen before is an apple or an orange. As a result, an ANN is comparable to a mathematical model that gains knowledge from instances to make predictions or categorical judgments, much as how you learned to tell an apple from an orange from your friend’s expertise.

ANNs can be used to solve various issues, including anomaly detection, dimensionality reduction, clustering, regression, classification, and more. ANNs can be used, for instance, to recognize handwritten numbers, identify diseases, forecast stock prices, produce natural language, etc. The versatility and scalability of ANNs and their capacity to represent non-linear and dynamic interactions are some of their benefits. They can also manage complex and noisy data.

On the other hand, high computational cost, lack of interpretability and explainability, and vulnerability to overfitting and local minima are some drawbacks of ANNs. Some more limitations are given below:

•Data and resource requirements: ANNs often require large amounts of labeled data to train effectively and avoid overfitting. This can be costly and time-consuming to collect and process. Moreover, ANNs can have millions or billions of parameters that must be updated during training, requiring high-performance hardware and software. The complexity and size of ANNs also make them difficult to deploy and maintain in real-world scenarios.

•Interpretability and explainability: ANNs are often black box models, producing outputs without revealing underlying logic or reasoning. This can pose challenges for understanding how ANNs make decisions, verifying their correctness, and debugging errors. Furthermore, ANNs may not be able to provide justifications or evidence for their outputs, which can affect the trust and acceptance of users and stakeholders. For example, an ANN that diagnoses a medical condition may be unable to explain why it chose a specific diagnosis or what features it considers relevant.

•Generalization and extrapolation: ANNs are designed to learn from data and generalize to unseen situations. However, this may not always be the case, especially when the data is noisy, biased, or insufficient. ANNs may overfit the training data and fail to perform well on new or different data. Alternatively, ANNs may underfit the data and fail to capture the underlying patterns or relationships. Moreover, ANNs may struggle to extrapolate from the data and handle novel or unexpected scenarios or facts. For example, an ANN that recognizes faces may not be able to identify a face with a mask or a face from a different ethnicity.

10.2.1Mathematical Model of an Artificial Neuron

A general mathematical model of an artificial neuron is shown in Fig. 10.1. Here, x1,x2∙∙∙, and xn. are the inputs the artificial neuron receives from an external source. The source can be a user-supplied input or features extracted from data. Each input is linked to the artificial neuron represented by a directed edge labeled with a suitable weight. Thus for the inputs x1,x2∙∙∙,xn the corresponding weights are w1,w2∙∙∙,wn... The artificial neuron has two parts: summation and activation. The summation is the sum of the products of the inputs and the corresponding weights. The resultant is given as input to the activation, which produces an output.

Figure 10.1  Mathematical model of an artificial neuron

The mathematical equation describing the process is shown below:

(10.1)

$t = \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}x_{i}w_{i}$

(10.2)

y = f(t)

The activation function can be considered a non-linear filter producing the output. The other commonly used activation functions are:

(10.3)

$f\left( t \right) = \left\{ \begin{matrix} {1,} & {t \geq \theta} \\ {0,} & {< \theta} \\ \end{matrix} \right.$

(10.4)

$f\left( t \right) = \frac{1}{\left( {1 + e^{- \alpha t}} \right)}$

(10.5)

$f\left( t \right) = \frac{e^{x} - e^{- x}}{e^{x} + e^{- x}}$

(10.6)

$f\left( t \right) = \left\{ \begin{matrix} {1,} & {t \geq 0} \\ {0,} & {t < 0} \\ \end{matrix} \right.$

The different types of activation functions, such as sigmoid (Equation 10.4), tanh (Equation 10.5), and ReLU (Equation 10.3) have different properties and applications.

Sigmoid function: This is the most commonly used activation function in neural networks. The need for a sigmoid function stems from many learning algorithms requiring the activation function to be differentiable and, hence, continuous. The step function is unsuitable in such situations as it is not continuous. To elaborate, an activation function is a mathematical function that transforms a neuron’s input into its output, which introduces non-linearity in the model, which in turn allows the neural network to learn more complex decision boundaries. The sigmoid function is one of the earliest and most commonly used (popular) activation functions, as it has some desirable properties:

•It is non-linear.

•It can be easily used in gradient-based optimization methods.

•It is easy to understand.

•It is easy to implement, as it has a simple formula.

The sigmoid function maps any input value to a value between 0 and 1 and is useful for binary classification and also for logistic regression problems. It is an S-shaped curve. As the input value increases, the output value starts with a slow increase in the beginning, then quickly approaches 1, and finally levels off. The sigmoid function also has some limitations:

•It can suffer from a vanishing gradient problem, meaning that the function’s gradient becomes very small when the input value is very large or small. This can slow down or even prevent the learning process of the network.

•It can cause saturation of neurons, which means that the function’s output becomes very close to 0 or 1 when the input value is very large or small. This can decrease the sensitivity of the network to changes in the input.

•It is not zero-centered, meaning the function’s output is always positive. This can introduce undesirable correlations in the gradients of adjacent layers and affect the network’s learning process.

Therefore, alternative activation functions, such as tanh, ReLU, leaky ReLU, etc., have been proposed to overcome these drawbacks. However, the sigmoid function remains a vital activation function in neural networks.

For example, an artificial neuron has two inputs x1 and x2, weights w1 and w2, and bias b. Its sigmoid activation function is shown below:

Output = sigmoid(w1 * x1 + w2 * x2 + b)

The output of this neuron will be a value between 0 and 1, depending on the inputs, weights, and bias values. For instance, if w1 = 0.5, w2 = -0.3, b = -0.2, x1 = 0.8, and x2 = 0.6, the output will be:

Output = sigmoid(0.5 * 0.8 -0.3 * 0.6 -0.2) = sigmoid(0.04) = 0.51

This means that these inputs activate this neuron slightly.

10.2.3The Perceptron Model

The perceptron model is used for data or pattern classification. The typical structure of a perceptron model to classify logical AND inputs is shown in Fig. 10.5.

Figure 10.5  Generalized perceptron model

The perceptron neuron takes multiple inputs along with a biased input, applies weight to each input, and computes the weighted sum. An activation function is applied to the weighted sum to determine the output.

Perceptron Algorithm

1.Initialize the weights to zero vector.

2.Take the first input and perform the sum of the products. Then apply the activation function.

3.If the predicted output matches the original output, do nothing

4.Adjust the weights using the perceptron learning rule if the predicted output does not match the actual output.

5.Consider the input that follows and repeat the process until one input cycle is completed.

6.Repeat the process defined in steps 2 to 5 until the algorithm converges.

The perceptron algorithm guarantees convergence if the data is linearly separable. The activation function used in perceptron is the threshold function defined in Equation (10.9).

(10.9)

$\hat{y} = \left\{ \begin{matrix} 1 & {\text{sum} \geq \theta} \\ {- 1} & {\text{sum} < \theta} \\ \end{matrix} \right.$.

Perceptron learning rule: If y ≠ ŷ then wi(new) = wi(old) + η × y × xi,

where η  =  learning  rate;  the  value  lies  between  [0,1]; y  =  actual  output;  xi  =  ith  input  pattern; wi(old) = weight vector of the ith input pattern;and wi(new) = adjusted weight vector ith input pattern.

10.2.4Gradient Descent

Gradient descent is a first-order optimization problem. The gradient is a generalization of the derivative of a function on several variables. If f (x1, x2∙∙∙,xn ) is a differentiable scalar function of several variables, its gradient is a vector whose components are n-partial derivatives of the function f.. Hence, it is a vector-valued function.

Gradient represents the slope of the tangent of the graph of the function. It points toward the greatest rate of increase of the function, and its magnitude is the slope of the graph. It finds a model’s optimal parameters or weights by minimizing the cost or loss function. It is an iterative process where the parameters are tuned to reach the optimal values in each iteration.

To find the local minimum of a function using gradient descent, we should take steps proportional to the negative of the function’s gradient at the current point. If we move towards the positive of the gradient, then we approach the function’s local maximum, termed gradient ascent.

Gradient descent is also known as steepest descent or method of steepest descent. The two requirements to use gradient descent are that the function should be differentiable and convex.

Gradient Descent Algorithm: The idea of the gradient descent algorithm is that in each iteration, the point that follows is calculated using the current point and a learning rate. It subtracts the value since we need to minimize the cost function. It is represented using the equation

pn + 1 = pn − η∇f(pn),

where pn is the current point, pn+1 is the next point, ŋ is the learning rate, and ∇f(pn) represents the gradient at the current point. The advantage of the learning rate is that it governs the convergence process. If the value is small, convergence is delayed. If it is a large value, convergence is not guaranteed.

For example, f (x) = x2 - 3x.

f′ (x) = 2x - 3 and f′′ (x) = 2,, which guarantees that the function is convex.

The plot of the function is depicted in Fig. 10.8.

Figure 10.8  Plot of the function x2 − 3x

You can observe that the function could not move further from point 1.5001 though the local minima are at 0. This is the smallest value we can reach from the gradient descent algorithm that is converged to 1.5001.

Gradient descent is a powerful optimization technique that iteratively updates the parameters of a model to minimize a loss function. However, it still faces some specific challenges that affect its performance:

•It can converge to local optima rather than global optima. This means that the algorithm may stop at a point where the loss function is not at its lowest value but rather at a local minimum surrounded by higher values. This can happen when the loss function is non-convex and has multiple minima.

•Learning rate value has a significant impact. The learning rate is a hyperparameter that controls how much the parameters are updated in each iteration. If the learning rate is too small, the algorithm may take too long to converge or get stuck in a plateau. If the learning rate is too large, the algorithm may overshoot the optimal point and diverge or oscillate.

•If the model is complex, overfitting issues will arise. Overfitting means the model performs well on the training data but poorly on new or unseen data. This can happen when the model has too many parameters or features that capture noise or irrelevant patterns in the data.

•The rate of convergence is slow for large data sets or in high-dimensional spaces. This is because gradient descent requires calculation of the gradient of the loss function concerning all the parameters in each iteration, which can be computationally expensive and time-consuming for large data sets or models with many features.

10.3Types of Artificial Neural Networks

Feedforward neural network (FNN): You can imagine this as a one-way street. Without any loops or feedback, information moves from the input to the output. It resembles a network of neurons carrying data in a single direction. Feedforward neural networks are frequently used for language processing or picture recognition.

Convolutional neural network (CNN): A CNN is used primarily to comprehend visual data, much like how our brain interprets images. It applies filters or ‘feature detectors’ to various portions of the image to find patterns and shapes. For instance, it may identify edges, corners, or textures in an image. CNNs are used in many different applications, including image categorization, object identification, and picture synthesis.

Recurrent neural network (RNN): An RNN is a memory-equipped network. It can handle text and other sequential data types like time series. It has links that create loops that let data flow back to earlier processes. This network remembers and considers previous data when making predictions. RNNs are frequently employed for sentiment analysis, speech recognition, and language translation.

Long short-term memory (LSTM) network: It is a form of RNN that excels at identifying long-term dependencies in sequential data. The ‘short-term memory’ constraint of conventional RNNs is addressed. Since LSTMs include specialized memory cells, they can process and retain pertinent information over longer sequences by selectively remembering or forgetting it at each step. Language modeling, speech recognition, and handwriting recognition are prominent applications of LSTMs.

Generative adversarial network (GAN): A GAN is a unique network where two models, a generator and a discriminator, are competitively pitted against one another. The generator attempts to produce artificial data, such as photographs, that closely resembles actual data, while the discriminator’s task is to tell the difference between the two. GANs may produce incredibly realistic data through this adversarial process, which makes them suitable for jobs like picture synthesis, video production, and data augmentation.

10.3.1Feedforward Neural Network (FNN)

Also called a multi-layer perceptron, here the information goes in a single path from the input layer through one or more hidden layers and eventually to the oput layer (Fig. 10.9). The input, hidden, and output layers are the three basic types of layers that make up an FNN’s architecture. Artificial neurons (nodes) that process and send information make up each layer. Input data, such as a sample’s characteristics, are sent to the input layer. Then, each neuron in the input layer represents one aspect of the input data.

Between the input and output layers lie what are known as hidden layers. To extract pertinent patterns and characteristics, they compute the incoming data. Depending on how complicated the problem is, both the total number of hidden layers as well as the total number of neurons in each layer may change.

Figure 10.9  Feedforward network (FFN)

The output layer produces the network’s ultimate output, which can be a prediction, classification, or regression value. The type of task determines how many neurons are present in the output layer. Each neuron in the output layer can represent a specific category, for instance, if the aim is to categorize photos into different groups. A weighted sum of inputs and an activation function are the two fundamental processes carried out by each neuron in an FNN.

Each input’s weight, which reflects its relative importance, is multiplied by the inputs from the preceding layer. The sum of these weighted inputs is calculated. The weighted total is then passed through an activation function, which causes the network to become non-linear. Based on the weighted total, the activation function determines whether or not to stimulate the neuron. It increases adaptability and enables the network to understand intricate connections between inputs and outputs.

Forward Propagation: Starting from the input layer, the forward propagation process entails moving the input data through the network’s hidden layers until it reaches the output layer. Each neuron computes its weighted sum to generate an output and applies the activation function. The process continues until it reaches the output layer, where these outputs serve as the inputs for the following layer.

Training: To train an FNN, we require a labelled data set that contains input data and the correct outputs they should produce. The network modifies the weights associated with each neuron throughout training to reduce the discrepancy between its predictions and the correct outputs. This is accomplished by measuring the network’s performance using a loss function and an optimization approach like gradient descent.

Consider this straightforward FNN example for handwritten digit recognition. Neurons in the input layer represent the pixels in an input image. The hidden layers process the input image to extract characteristics like edges, curves, or patterns. The output layer is made up of 10 neurons, each of which represents a digit from 0 to 9. The neuron in the output layer with the highest activity value indicates the projected digit. This FNN learns to connect the input patterns with the associated digits by being trained on a data set of labeled handwritten digits. Once trained, it can recognize handwritten numbers even in previously unobserved images.

FNNs are adaptable and frequently used for various tasks, including natural language processing, picture recognition, and many other applications that call for pattern detection and prediction.

10.3.2Convolutional Neural Networks

The convolutional neural network, also called CNN, is a type of ANN that can process complicated and high-dimensional input, including sounds, pictures, videos, and spoken language. CNNs are explicitly created to analyse and comprehend visual data, much as how our brains do.

CNNs comprise several layers, such as convolution, pooling, activation, and fully connected layers, which each execute a distinct action on the input data.

Convolutional Layer: The convolutional layer is a fundamental component of a CNN. It comprises several feature detectors or filters that slide methodically over the input image. Each filter employs a convolutional mathematical operation to identify specific patterns or features, such as edges, textures, or forms. Convolution involves multiplying the filter weights by the matching pixel values and applying the filter to a small image area at a time. The resulting values are added together to provide a single value indicating whether a specific feature is present in that area. A new feature map highlighting the identified features is created by repeating this process throughout the image.

Pooling Layer: A CNN frequently adds a pooling layer after the convolutional layer. This layer decreases the feature maps’ dimensionality while the crucial details are preserved. It makes the network more resistant to changes in the size or position of the identified features. Max pooling is the most frequently used pooling method. The most significant value is picked for each smaller region on the feature map. By doing this, the size of the feature map is reduced while maintaining the most crucial information.

Convolutional and pooling layers are typically followed by one or more fully linked layers at the end of a CNN. These layers resemble those in a conventional feedforward neural network, where every neuron is coupled to every neuron in the layer before it.

Neuron Operations: Just like in a typical neural network, the neurons in the fully connected layer calculate weighted sums of the inputs from the preceding layer and send the results through an activation function. The activations in these neurons represent the network’s ultimate output.

Training: A labeled data set containing input images and their related labels is utilized for training a CNN. Like other neural networks, the network modifies its biases and weights during training to reduce discrepancies between its predictions and the correct labels. This is accomplished using an appropriate loss function and optimization techniques like gradient descent.

Let us look at an example of a CNN for image classification that can differentiate between cats and dogs. The pixel values of an input image are taken in by a layer that is part of the CNN. The successive convolutional layers would identify various aspects of the image, such as edges, textures, or forms. Thanks to the pooling layers, the feature maps would be downscaled while still containing the necessary data. By being trained on a collection of labeled cat and dog photographs, this CNN learns to connect the visual patterns of cats and dogs with their corresponding labels. In addition, it correctly identifies new, unseen photos of a dog or a cat after being trained.

CNNs can also generalize their learning from a lot of data to fresh and unstudied material. CNNs take their cues from the biological design and operation of the brain’s visual cortex, which comprises neurons that respond to various visual field stimuli. The basis of CNNs is the kernels, sometimes referred to as filters. Using the convolution approach, kernels extract the crucial data from the input.

10.3.2.1Convolutional Layer

The convolutional layer in a CNN performs a mathematical operation called convolution on the input data (Fig. 10.10).

Figure 10.10  Convolutional layer

Convolution means applying a filter, also known as a kernel, to a local region of the input data and producing an output value that is the weighted sum of the filter and the input values. The filter slides over the input data, moving by a certain number of steps called strides, and produces an output matrix called a feature map. The feature map captures the spatial patterns and features of the input data relevant to the task at hand (Fig. 10.11).

Figure 10.11  Image representation in a matrix

Figure 10.12  Convolution logic in the matrix format

Let us have an input image of size 6 x 6 pixels. We want to apply a convolutional layer with a filter of size 3 x 3 pixels and a stride of 1. The filter will slide over the input image, starting from the top-left corner, and produce an output value for each 3 x 3 region of the image. The output feature map will contain information about the edges, corners, and shapes of the input image detected by the filter (Fig. 10.12).

A convolutional layer can have multiple filters, each producing a different feature map. The feature maps are stacked together along the depth dimension to form the output volume of the convolutional layer. The filters can have different sizes, strides, and padding options to control the shape and size of the output volume. The filters are also learnable parameters that are updated during the training process to optimize the performance of the CNN.

10.3.2.2Pooling Layer

The size of the feature maps generated by the convolutional layers is reduced by a pooling layer, which is a part of a CNN. The principal advantages of pooling are that it enhances network efficiency and avoids overfitting by reducing the number of parameters and computations. It improves generalization and translation invariance by making the network more resilient to changes in the location and orientation of the features in the input image.

The most frequently used pooling procedures are average and maximum pooling. There are other forms as well. While average pooling determines the average value, maximum pooling chooses the maximum value in each area of the feature map that is filtered. For example, if we apply a 2 x 2 max pooling filter with a stride of 2 to a 4 x 4 feature map, we get a 2 x 2 output as shown in Fig. 10.13.

Figure 10.13  Pooling by choosing maximum

If we apply a 2 x 2 average pooling filter with a stride of 2 to a 4 x 4 feature map, we get a 2 x 2 output as shown in Fig. 10.14.

Figure 10.14  Pooling by choosing the average

The most noticeable features in each region are preserved by max pooling, while the features are rounded off by average pooling. Both approaches can aid in reducing noise and extraneous information in feature maps. The highest or average value over the entire spatial dimension is used in global pooling, which reduces each channel of the feature map to a single value (Fig. 10.15).

Figure 10.15  Single-value pooling

This can be helpful for producing a compact representation of the features or for lowering the number of parameters needed before a fully connected layer.

In a CNN architecture, pooling layers are typically positioned after one or more convolutional layers. Depending on the desired level of down sampling, they can have various filter sizes and strides. Pooling layers are a fundamental component of CNNs and are crucial for removing significant features from images.

Advantages: Pooling layers are a common component of CNNs, which are widely used for image recognition and classification tasks. Pooling layers perform a subsampling operation on the feature maps produced by the convolutional layers, which results in several advantages for the CNN model. The three main advantages of pooling layers are dimensionality reduction, translation invariance, and feature selection.

Dimensionality reduction refers to the process of reducing the number of dimensions or variables in a data set or a model. This can help in improving the efficiency and performance of the model, as well as preventing overfitting. Overfitting occurs when the model learns too much from the training data and fails to generalize well to new or unseen data. By reducing the spatial dimensions of the feature maps, pooling layers can lower the computational cost and memory usage of the model, as well as reduce the number of parameters that need to be learned.

Translation invariance is another important property that pooling layers can help achieve in CNNs. Translation invariance means that the model is able to recognize and classify an object in an image regardless of its position or location in the image. This is desirable because we want the model to be robust to slight variations or shifts in the input image, which are common in real-world scenarios. Pooling layers can provide translation invariance by aggregating or summarizing the information from a local neighborhood of pixels in the feature map..

Feature selection is the process of selecting or extracting the most relevant or informative features from the input data for a specific task or goal. This can help in improving the accuracy and interpretability of the model, as well as reducing noise and redundancy. Pooling layers can perform feature selection by applying a non-linear function to the feature maps, which enhances or suppresses certain features based on their importance or relevance.

Disadvantages: The first disadvantage of pooling layers is that they cause information loss. Pooling layers apply a function, such as max or average, to a local region of the feature map and output a single value. This means that some information from the input feature map is discarded, which can be necessary for the final classification or regression task. The second disadvantage of pooling layers is that they can cause over-smoothing of the feature maps. Pooling layers reduce the spatial resolution of the feature maps, which can result in the loss of some fine-grained details that are important for the final classification or regression task.

The third disadvantage of pooling layers is that they introduce hyperparameters that need to be tuned in order to achieve optimal performance. Pooling layers have two main hyperparameters: the size of the pooling regions and the stride. The size of the pooling regions determines how much spatial information is aggregated and reduced in each output feature map. The stride determines how much the pooling regions are shifted along the input feature map. Both hyperparameters affect the trade-off between computational efficiency and representational power of the feature maps. If we use a small pooling region or a small stride, we can preserve more spatial information and obtain more output feature maps, but at the cost of more computation and memory. If we use a large pooling region or a large stride, we can reduce the computation and memory requirements, but at the cost of losing more spatial information and obtaining fewer output feature maps. Therefore, finding the optimal values for these hyperparameters requires some trial and error and some expertise in model building.

10.3.2.3Activation Functions

In a CNN, the output of a convolutional layer is subjected to mathematical operations known as activation functions. They give the network non-linearity, which enables it to recognize intricate patterns and characteristics in the input data. In addition, the range and size of the output values, which might impact the network’s performance and stability, are also controlled by activation functions. In CNNs, various activation function types can be applied, each with unique benefits and drawbacks. The most typical ones are discussed below.

Sigmoid: This function with an S-shaped curve known as the sigmoid curve converts the result to a probability that may be understood as a value between 0 and 1. It is helpful for binary classification tasks like face identification or image segmentation. However, it has the vanishing gradient issue, which makes it challenging to update the weights during backpropagation because the gradient gets extremely small for significant positive or negative values. Other advantageous characteristics of the sigmoid function include its differentiability, monotonicity, and single inflection point. The logistic function, outlined as follows, is one of the most used sigmoid functions.

f(x) = 1 / (1 + e^(-x)),

where x is any real value and e is the natural logarithm’s base.

The logistic function’s graph appears as shown in Fig. 10.16.

Figure 10.16  Logistic function graph

As you can see, as x approaches negative and positive infinity, the logistic function approaches 0 and 1, respectively. The inflection point, located at y = 0.5, is also a horizontal asymptote of the logistic function. This logistic function is frequently utilized in ML, particularly in logistic regression and ANNs. The logistic function can be employed in ANNs as a neuron’s activation function, dictating how much a neuron fires in response to input. The behavior of biological neurons, which have a firing threshold and a saturation point, can be modeled using the logistic function. In addition, the network can learn more complex patterns by adding non-linearity using the logistic function.

Tanh: This function, considered a scaled sigmoid function, maps the output to a value between 1 and 1. It also works well for classification jobs since it generates zero-centered results that can be instructive. However, it still has the vanishing gradient issue, although somewhat less than the sigmoid function. One of the hyperbolic functions, or trigonometric equivalents, is the tanh function, defined by utilizing a hyperbola rather than a circle. The ratio of sinh and cosh, the hyperbolic sine and cosine functions, is known as the tanh function. The tanh formula is:

tanh (x) = sinh (x) divided by cosh (x)

As an alternative, we can define tanh as follows using the exponential function:

tanh(x) is equal to (ex - e-x) / (ex + e-x)

Some intriguing features of the tanh function include:

•Because it is an odd function, tanh(-x) always equals -tanh(x) regardless of x.

•Its range is (-1, 1). Hence, it can never go above or below these numbers.

•As x approaches infinity, it has a horizontal asymptote at y = 1, while as x approaches negative infinity, it has one at y = -1.

•It has a period of pi * i, where i is the fictitious and periodic unit.

ReLU: This stands for rectified linear unit. It is a type of activation function that is commonly used in CNNs. Activation functions are mathematical operations that determine the output of a neuron based on its input. ReLU has a simple formula: f(x) = max(0, x). This means it takes the maximum of zero and the input value and returns it as the output. For example, if the input is -2, the output is 0; if the input is 3, the output is 3. ReLU has several advantages over other activation functions. First, it is fast and easy to compute since it only involves a comparison operation. Second, it is efficient since it reduces the computational complexity of the network by sparsifying the output. Third, it helps to overcome the vanishing gradient problem, which occurs when the gradients of the network become very small and prevent learning. This happens because some activation functions, such as sigmoid or tanh, have outputs bounded between -1 and 1, and their derivatives are close to zero for large inputs. ReLU, conversely, has an unbounded output for positive inputs, and its derivative is either 0 or 1. This means it preserves the gradient for positive inputs and allows learning to continue.

However, ReLU also has some drawbacks. One is the dying ReLU problem, which occurs when some neurons stop learning and become inactive. This happens because ReLU has a zero output and a zero derivative for negative inputs. If a neuron receives only negative inputs for a long time, it will never fire, and its weights will not be updated. This can lead to a loss of information and a reduction of the network’s expressive power. To avoid this problem, some variants of ReLU have been proposed, such as leaky ReLU or parametric ReLU, which have a slight positive slope for negative inputs.

Leaky ReLU is an activation function which simply returns the input if it is positive or zero if it is negative. However, ReLU has a drawback known as the dying ReLU problem, which means that some neurons can become inactive and stop learning if they receive only negative inputs for a long time. This can reduce the expressive power and accuracy of the network. To address this issue, leaky ReLU introduces a slight positive slope for negative inputs instead of setting them to zero. This means that the output of leaky ReLU is either the input itself if it is positive or a fraction of the input if it is negative. The fraction is usually chosen to be 0.01, but it can be any small positive number. By doing this, leaky ReLU allows some gradient to flow through the negative values, which helps to keep the neurons alive and learning. For example, if the input is -5, the output of ReLU is 0, but the output of leaky ReLU is -0.05.

Leaky ReLU can improve the stability and performance of CNNs, especially for deeper networks with many layers. Leaky ReLU can prevent the vanishing gradient problem, which occurs when the gradients become too small to update the weights effectively as they propagate through multiple layers. Leaky ReLU can also reduce the overfitting problem by introducing some noise and randomness into the network, which acts as a form of regularization.

Softmax: This function converts the output to a vector of values, which range from 0 to 1, adding up to 1. It is a generalization of the sigmoid function for multi-class classification problems like image recognition or natural language processing. Each class label is given a probability based on the output values’ relative magnitudes. It is typically paired with a cross-entropy loss function as the final activation function in CNNs. For example, we have an image recognition problem where we want to classify an image into one of four categories: cat, dog, bird, or fish. We can use a CNN to extract features from the image and produce a vector of output values, one for each category. However, these output values are not probabilities and may not be in the same range. To convert them into possibilities, we can apply the softmax function.

The softmax function works by exponentiating each output value and dividing it by the sum of all exponentiated values. This way, larger output values will have higher probabilities, and smaller output values will have lower probabilities. The softmax function also has the property that it is invariant to adding or subtracting a constant from the output vector, which means that it does not depend on the absolute magnitude of the output values but only on their relative differences. For example, suppose the output vector from the CNN is [2.3, 1.2, -0.8, 0.5]. We get [0.57, 0.21, 0.03, 0.18] if we apply the softmax function. These are the probabilities that the image belongs to each category. We can see that the softmax function assigns the highest probability to the first category (cat) and the lowest probability to the third category (bird). The sum of all probabilities is 1.

The softmax function is often used as the final activation function in CNNs for multi-class classification problems. This means we can compare the predicted probabilities with the true labels using a loss function after applying the softmax function. The cross-entropy loss function is a common loss function which measures how well the predicted probabilities match the true labels. The cross-entropy loss function penalizes predictions that are confident but wrong and rewards predictions that are confident and correct. For example, suppose the true label for the image is a cat (the first category). The cross-entropy loss function would compute the negative logarithm of the predicted probability for the cat, which is -log(0.57) = 0.56. This relatively low loss value indicates that the prediction is close to the true label. On the other hand, if the true label were a bird (the third category), the cross-entropy loss function would compute -log(0.03) = 3.51. This is a high loss value, indicating that the prediction is far from the true label.

We can train the CNN to learn the optimal parameters that produce accurate predictions for new images by minimizing the cross-entropy loss function over a training set of images and labels.

10.3.2.4Training CNNs

CNN can analyze structured data like text, audio, or images. Multiple layers make up CNNs, each applying a distinct operation to the input data. These operations include convolution, pooling, activation, normalization, and drop out. A CNN’s objective is to extract from the data hierarchical features that may be applied to various tasks, including classification, segmentation, detection, and generation.

Picture classification or giving a name to a picture based on its content, is one of the most popular uses of CNNs. When a CNN is being trained, the model is fed with the images and their labels, and the layer weights are adjusted using an optimization algorithm like stochastic gradient descent (SGD) or Adam. A loss function that calculates the discrepancy between the predicted and actual labels is the object of the optimization algorithm’s attempt to minimize it. For example, cross-entropy, mean squared error or hinge loss are some loss functions that can be chosen based on the task and the data.

Steps in the training process

1.Use a pre-trained model or random seeding to set the layer weights.

2.Rearrange and divide the data set into groups of labels and images.

3.Carry out the following actions for every batch:

a.Forward pass: Run the photos through the model’s layers and calculate the predicted outputs.

b.Backward pass: Determine the gradients of the loss function concerning the weights using the chain rule.

c.Update: Use the optimization algorithm and a learning rate parameter to update the weights.

4.Continue performing steps 2 and 3 until the loss function converges or a predetermined number of epochs (iterations across the entire data set) has been reached.

A CNN’s performance can be assessed using several criteria: accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. These metrics can be calculated distinct from the training set validation or test sets. The model’s hyperparameters, such as the learning rate, batch size, and number of epochs, can be adjusted using the validation set. The test set can be used to gauge how well the model generalizes to new data.

10.3.2.5Transfer Learning in CNN

An ML model can use the knowledge gained from one job to help with another using transfer learning. Transfer learning can be applied to CNNs to enhance the effectiveness and efficiency of image recognition models.

Using a pre-trained CNN model as a feature extractor or fine-tuner for a new job is the primary concept of transfer learning. A pre-trained CNN model is a model that has learned to extract standard and advanced features from images after being trained on a substantial and varied data set, such as ImageNet. These attributes can be helpful for many different image identification tasks, such as object detection, face recognition, or image segmentation. In addition, using a pre-trained CNN model allows us to take advantage of the existing knowledge of the model without training a new model from scratch, which can be expensive and time-consuming.

Feature extraction and fine-tuning are two typical applications of transfer learning in CNNs. We merely train a new classifier on top of the pre-trained CNN model as a fixed feature extractor during feature extraction. This scenario is appropriate when the new task significantly differs from the previous task or has a short data set. For instance, we can use a pre-trained CNN model to extract features from the photographs and then train a straightforward linear classifier on top of them if we want to categorize flowers based on a small data set of flower images. During training, we update some or all of the parameters of the pre-trained CNN model as we fine-tune it. This scenario is appropriate when the new work includes a sizable data set or is similar to the old task.

Transfer learning applications in CNNs:

•FaceNet: This CNN model is trained on a large data set of face images with labels indicating whether two faces belong to the same person. The model can then be used for specific face recognition tasks such as face verification, face clustering, and face alignment by fine-tuning it on a smaller data set of target faces. For example, FaceNet can be used to verify whether two photos show the same person by comparing their embeddings in the Euclidean space.

•Mask R-CNN: This CNN model performs instance segmentation, identifying and classifying every object in an image and generating a pixel-level mask for each object. The model builds on a previously trained CNN model for object detection, such as Faster R-CNN, and then adds a new branch for segmentation mask prediction. The model can be further fine-tuned on a data set of images with annotated masks for different classes of objects. For example, Mask R-CNN can segment and label every person, car, tree, and building in an aerial image.

•Style transfer: This method creates a new image by joining the content of one image with the style of another image using transfer learning. The method extracts content and style features from the two images using a pre-trained CNN model, such as VGG-19, trained on a large data set of natural images for image classification. Using gradient descent, the method then optimizes a new image to match the original image’s content and style features. For example, style transfer can be used to create an artistic image that blends the content of a cityscape photo with the style of Van Gogh’s Starry Night painting.

10.3.2.6Applications of CNNs

CNNs are widely used in many fields, including computer vision, natural language processing (NLP), audio processing, and biomedical imaging. Some examples of CNN applications are as follows:

•Face recognition: CNNs can learn to recognize faces in pictures or videos and compare them to a database of recognized individuals. This can be applied to social networking, security, or authentication needs. For example, Facebook uses a CNN called DeepFace to identify and tag people in photos. DeepFace can achieve 97.35% accuracy on a standard face recognition benchmark.

•Image captioning: CNNs can produce natural language descriptions of images by fusing visual and linguistic data. Accessibility, education, or enjoyment can all be achieved with this. For example, Google Photos uses a CNN called Show and Tell to generate captions for user-uploaded photos. Show and Tell can produce relevant, informative, and grammatically correct captions.

•Object detection: CNNs can identify and categorize things in pictures or movies using bounding boxes or masks. This can be utilized for robotics, autonomous driving, or spying. For example, YOLO (You Only Look Once) is a CNN that can detect and localize multiple objects in real-time video streams. YOLO can achieve 45% mean average precision on a standard object detection benchmark.

•Style transfer: CNNs can use feature representations learned from many layers to transfer one image’s style to another. Artistic, imaginative, or personalized uses can be made of this. For example, Neural Style Transfer is a technique that can apply the style of a painting to a photograph. Neural Style Transfer can create images that are visually appealing and expressive.

•Medical diagnosis: CNNs can analyze images from diagnostic tests like X-rays, MRIs, and ultrasounds to find anomalies or diseases. This may be applied to medical care, diagnosis, or therapy. For example, CheXNet is a CNN that can diagnose 14 different thoracic diseases from chest X-ray images. CheXNet can outperform radiologists on some diseases and achieve comparable performance on others.

CNNs are solid and adaptable tools that can manage complex and varied data. As a result, they continue to stimulate new research and innovation while revolutionizing numerous fields and applications.

10.3.3Recurrent Neural Networks

Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are a subset of ANNs capable of processing sequential data, including speech, video, and natural language. RNNs can manage variable-length inputs and outputs by keeping an internal state that depends on the prior inputs, unlike feedforward neural networks, which have fixed input and output sizes. As a result, RNNs can pick up temporal patterns in the data and learn long-term dependencies. RNNs are frequently employed for sentiment analysis, speech recognition, and language translation.

Memory and Feedback: The capacity of an RNN to retain memory or context about the prior information it has encountered in the sequence is one of its fundamental characteristics. This memory is made possible by using feedback connections, which allow data from earlier phases in the sequence to be relayed back into the network. An RNN has a hidden state that serves as its context or memory. The RNN receives an input at each step in the sequence and generates an output based on the input at that point in the sequence and the hidden state from the previous step. At each step, the hidden state is updated with data from both the current input and the previous hidden state. The RNN processes the sequence one step at a time, incorporating the input at each stage and altering the hidden state as necessary. As a result, it can recognize patterns and dependencies in the data throughout time because it uses the same set of weights and biases for each sequence step.

RNNS are composed of recurrent units, which are straightforward computational units that accept an input vector and produce an output vector. Each recurrent unit also has a hidden state vector that keeps data from earlier inputs. A non-linear function is applied to the current input and the initial hidden state to update the vector at each time step. The hidden state vector is then used to generate the output vector, with the option of utilizing another non-linear function.

The issue of disappearing or exploding gradients, which occurs when the gradients of the loss function concerning the network parameters become very tiny or very big during backpropagation, is one of the fundamental difficulties RNNs face. As a result, it is challenging to train RNNs on lengthy sequences since the gradients frequently decay or increase exponentially with time. Several approaches have been put forth to solve this issue, including gradient clipping, LSTM (long short-term memory) units, GRUs (gated recurrent units), and attention mechanisms.

CNN and RNN differ in some ways:

•CNN is designed for processing spatial data, such as images, videos, or 2D/3D shapes. RNN is designed for processing sequential data, such as text, speech, or time series.

•CNN has no memory of the previous inputs, and can only learn local features from the data. RNN has memory cells that store the previous states, and can learn long-term dependencies from the data.

•CNN requires fixed-size inputs and outputs, which means that the data has to be padded or cropped to fit the network. RNN can handle variable-length inputs and outputs, which means that the network can adapt to the data dynamically.

•CNN is more specialized, effective, rigid, and constrained, which means that it can perform well on specific tasks, but it is hard to generalize to other domains or tasks. RNN is more adaptable, generalizable, complex, and prone to overfitting and vanishing gradients, which means that it can learn from diverse data sources, but it is also more difficult to train and optimize.

For example, CNN can be used for image classification, object detection, face recognition, or semantic segmentation. RNN can be used for natural language processing, speech recognition, machine translation, or text generation.

10.3.3.1Long Short-Term Memory Networks

This is a type of RNN that can recognize long-term dependencies in sequential input. RNNs are neural networks that handle sequential data by iterating over a hidden state that encodes the inputs that came before. However, the disappearing and ballooning gradient issues that RNNs experience make it challenging to learn long-term dependencies. Three gates that regulate the information flow in and out of the memory cell and a memory cell that can store and update information over time are used in LSTM networks to solve these issues: the input gate, the forget gate, and the output gate ( Fig. 10.17).

Figure 10.17  LSTM logic

The output gate determines what data should be output from the cell, the input gate determines what new data should be added, and the forget gate determines what outdated data should be removed from the cell. As a result, LSTM networks can learn intricate and persistent patterns in sequential data, including speech, video, and spoken language.

10.3.3.2Gated Recurrent Unit Networks

The vanishing or expanding gradient issue with RNNs makes it challenging to understand long-term dependencies. To solve this issue, reset and update gates are two types used in gated recurrent unit (GRU) networks (Fig. 10.18).

Figure 10.18  Gated recurrent unit network

These gates regulate how much data is remembered or lost from the current input and the initial hidden state. GRU networks perform better than regular RNNs on many tasks because they may be trained to recall or forget relevant information over lengthy sequences selectively.

10.3.3.3Training RNNs

A labeled data set with sequential data and accompanying labels is used to train an RNN. Like other neural networks, the RNN modifies its weights and biases during training to reduce the discrepancy between its predictions and the accurate labels. This is accomplished using an appropriate loss function and optimization techniques like gradient descent. The issue of vanishing or exploding gradients, which arises during backpropagation through time (BPTT), occurs when the gradient of the loss function concerning the network parameters becomes very tiny or very large. The network may either learn very slowly due to this, or it may become unstable and diverge. Many solutions have been put out to address this issue, including regularization, gradient clipping, and advanced RNN designs like LSTM and GRU.

10.3.3.4Applications of RNNs

NLP, speech recognition, machine translation, text synthesis, image captioning, video analysis, and music composition are just a few of the tasks for which RNNs have been successfully used. In addition, RNNs are frequently combined with other neural network architectures, including transformers and CNNs, to benefit from the advantages of each model. As a result, RNNs are among the most powerful and adaptable deep learning technologies, constantly inspiring new research and applications.

RNNs can process time series, voice, audio, video, and other sequential data. RNNs can mimic complicated and dynamic processes because of their memory mechanism, which enables them to store and use data from earlier inputs. NLP, speech recognition, machine translation, text generation, sentiment analysis, picture captioning, video analysis, music synthesis, and other fields and applications have extensively used RNNs.

A group of units, or neurons, coupled recurrently to create a directed cycle make up RNNs. At every time step, each unit receives an input vector and outputs an output vector and a hidden state vector. The subsequent time step’s input for the same unit, or additional units, includes the hidden state vector. In this manner, the hidden state vector serves as a memory to store the history of the inputs. Depending on the job, the output vector may be used to anticipate the next word in a sentence, produce an answer to a question, or categorize an emotion.

The Elman network, often known as the simple recurrent network (SRN), is one of the most straightforward and extensively utilized RNN architectures. Each unit in this design has three sets of weights: recurrent weights that connect the hidden state vector to itself, output weights that connect the hidden state vector to the output vector, and input weights that connect the input vector to the hidden state vector. First, the weighted sum of the input vector and the preceding hidden state vector is used to calculate the hidden state vector, which is then calculated using a non-linear activation function (such as sigmoid or tanh). Finally, the output vector is calculated by adding another activation function, such as softmax, to the weighted sum of the hidden state vector.

One of its key features is RNN’s capacity to recognize long-term dependencies and context information in sequential data. RNNs, for instance, may learn a language’s syntactic and semantic norms and produce coherent and insightful phrases when used in natural language processing. However, one of the fundamental problems with RNNs is that they have trouble learning long-term relationships because of the vanishing or expanding gradient problem. This issue arises when, as the error function propagates over time, the gradient with regard to the weights becomes extremely tiny or extremely big, making it difficult to efficiently update the weights. This issue may lead RNNs to forget or disregard data from far-off inputs, or it may cause them to become unstable and give irregular outputs.

Many RNN variants and extensions, including LSTM networks, GRUs, bidirectional RNNs (BRNNs), attention mechanisms, and transformer networks, have been proposed to address this issue. These architectures introduce various mechanisms to regulate information flow and gradients through time, including gates that modulate each unit’s input and output, connections that skip over some time steps, alignments that concentrate on important input sequence segments, and self-attention that recognizes interdependent relationships between all inputs on a global scale.

RNN research and development is still ongoing in ML and AI. Current issues and potential directions for RNN research are as follows:

•Increasing RNNs’ scalability and effectiveness for large-scale applications.

•Creating new architectures and methods to manage sequential data that is multimodal and heterogeneous.

•Looking at new areas and uses where RNNs can offer fresh perspectives and answers.

•Improving RNNs’ interpretability and explainability for increased confidence and understanding.

•Including human feedback and prior knowledge in learning and creating RNNs.

RNNs are practical modeling tools for sequential events and data. Impressive outcomes have been shown in a variety of applications and fields. However, they also encounter some restrictions and difficulties that call for additional study and invention. Nevertheless, we can open up new avenues and prospects for artificial intelligence and machine learning by expanding RNN research.

10.3.3.5Challenges of RNNs

Another method for assisting RNNs in focusing on the essential elements of the input sequence for each output is attention mechanisms. They give each input a weight or score based on how much it contributes to the output. The output layer is then fed a weighted average or summary of the input sequence created using these weights. In this manner, they can identify long-term dependencies without relying on the network’s concealed state.

RNNs can be improved with external memory modules that can store and retrieve data over extended periods using memory networks, a more recent technique. These memory modules are accessible through network-controlled read-and-write operations. This enables individuals to save information such as facts, regulations, or general knowledge necessary to complete challenging tasks requiring deduction and reasoning.

The issue of gradient vanishing or exploding presents an additional challenge for RNNs. As a result, learning can become sluggish or unstable during training because the gradients or mistakes utilized to update the network parameters can become extremely small or very big. This occurs when RNNs multiply numerous matrices across several time steps to compute the gradients using BPTT. These matrices will exhibit exponential growth or contraction when the gradients spread throughout the network if their values are near zero or one.

The use of gradient clipping, regularization, or initialization approaches are a few solutions to this issue. Gradient clipping is a straightforward technique that restricts the gradients’ magnitude by scaling them up or down if they go beyond a predetermined limit. This stops them from getting too big or too little and creating numerical problems. Another technique that lessens overfitting and enhances generalization is regularization.

10.3.4Generative AI

Generative AI is a branch of artificial intelligence that focuses on creating new content or data from scratch, such as images, text, music, code, etc. It is important for several reasons: it can help us explore new possibilities and scenarios that we might not be able to imagine or simulate otherwise. For example, generative AI can create realistic images of faces that do not exist or generate novel designs for products, buildings, or artworks. It can augment our creativity and productivity by providing us with inspiration, feedback, or assistance. It can help us generate high-quality data for various purposes, such as training other AI models, testing software or systems, or conducting research or analysis. For example, generative AI can produce synthetic data that mimics real-world data but preserves privacy and security.

There are different types of generative AI models: generative adversarial networks (GANs), variational autoencoders (VAEs), and transformer models. We will look at GANs and VAEs in detail.

Transformer models signify a revolutionary advancement in ML. Their distinctive architecture, which allows for concurrent processing of sequences, deviates from the sequential data processing of conventional models. The research community is currently engaged in studying the mechanisms of transformers and these endeavors instill optimism regarding the future of transformer models. For more details, see Chapter 11.

10.3.4.1Generative Adversarial Networks

This type of neural network can output realistic and diverse data from input. A GAN consists of two components: a discriminator and a generator (Fig. 10.19). The discriminator’s objective is to correctly classify the data, while the generator’s objective is to deceive the discriminator. The generator aims to create fake data that resembles correct data, while the discriminator strives to distinguish between real and fake data. In the adversarial training process, the discriminator and the generator compete with one another to become more effective.

Figure 10.19  Generative adversarial network (GAN)

Numerous fields, including computer vision, NLP, audio synthesis, and others use GANs. GANs, for instance, can produce lifelike images of people, animals, landscapes, and even artwork. In addition, GANs can improve low-resolution photos, eliminate noise from photographs, or exchange styles between images. Furthermore, GANs can be used in NLP to produce text, such as captions, summaries, stories, or dialogue. Creating speech or music from text or other inputs is another application of GANs.

Training GANs: The discriminator and the generator are trained antagonistically, with the discriminator trying to catch the generator and the generator trying to trick the discriminator. The objective/goal is to achieve a state where the discriminator cannot distinguish between the data produced by the generator and the actual data.

One of the basic concepts of GAN training is the loss function, which measures how well the generator and the discriminator perform. This is because the generator tries to fool the discriminator by producing fake data that look like accurate data while the discriminator tries to distinguish between real and fake data. The loss function reflects the trade-off between these two objectives.

Another essential concept is regularization, which prevents overfitting or underfitting by adding some constraints or penalties to the model parameters or outputs. For example, overfitting occurs when a model memorizes the training data and cannot generalize to new input. At the same time, underfitting occurs when the model needs to be more complex and capture the complexity of the data. Regularization can help balance the model’s complexity and simplicity, thereby improving its generalization performance.

Evaluation metrics measure the quality and diversity of the generated data. Evaluating GANs is challenging because a clear definition of what makes a sound generation needs to be precise.

Methods to improve GAN training: Let us look at some state-of-the-art methods for improving GAN training in low-data regimes. One such method is data augmentation, which increases the amount and diversity of data by applying some transformations or perturbations to the existing data. For example, one can rotate, crop, flip, or change the color/brightness of an image to create a new image. Data augmentation can reduce overfitting and improve the robustness and diversity of the generated data.

Another method is self-supervised learning, which is learning good representations from unlabeled data by solving additional tasks that do not require human annotations. For example, one can predict the rotation angle, color, or location of an image patch as a self-supervised task. Self-supervised learning can extract meaningful features from limited data and improve the quality and realism of the generated data. A third method is transfer learning, which leverages knowledge from a pre-trained model on a large-scale data set to a new model on a smaller-scale data set.

Applications: GANs have been used in various fields, including creating 3D objects, video prediction, and images. Image generation is one of the most widely used uses of GANs. Realistic and varied images of human faces, animals, landscapes, and other subjects can be produced with GANs.

A GAN that can produce high-quality images of human faces with various styles and characteristics is StyleGAN. It can also modify existing photographs by altering their age, gender, expression, and hair color. Another illustration is the image-to-image translator CycleGAN, which can change images such as pictures into paintings, horses into zebras, summer into winter, etc.

Challenges: GAN training is a complex undertaking as we may encounter several difficulties that may compromise their performance and stability:

•Mode collapse: When the generator only provides a small range of outputs, or even the same output for various inputs, mode collapse occurs. This indicates that the generator only concentrates on a few modes that potentially trick the discriminator and lead to failure to represent the diversity of accurate data distribution. Mode collapse can result from several issues, including an imbalance between the generator and discriminator, a poor choice of the objective function, or incorrect parameter initialization. Among the potential remedies to stop or lessen mode collapse are:

●Wasserstein loss: This alternative objective function gauges the separation between the actual and fictitious data distributions instead of their overlap. Even when the discriminator is excellent or perfect, Wasserstein loss enables a gradient signal for the generator that is smoother and more insightful.

●Unrolled GANs: This method adjusts the generator loss function to consider both the outputs of the present discriminator and those of upcoming discriminator iterations. This prevents the generator from over-optimizing for a single discriminator and forces it to consider a longer-term viewpoint.

●Minibatch discrimination: This technique allows the discriminator to compare various samples within a minibatch instead of examining them separately. This enables the discriminator to identify mode collapse and gives the generator more enlightening input.

•Lack of convergence: When the generator and the discriminator oscillate or diverge during training instead of reaching a stable equilibrium, this is called non-convergence. As a result, the generator may produce subpar or erroneous outputs, or it may not be possible to draw valid conclusions from the data. Numerous factors, including an improper learning rate, an imbalance between the generator’s and the discriminator’s designs, or an unsuitable optimization algorithm, can lead to non-convergence. The following are some potential ways to strengthen or guarantee convergence:

●Gradient penalty: Based on the gradient norm of the discriminator, this regularization method adds a penalty term to the objective function. This is beneficial to prevent gradient explosion or vanishing and enforce a smoothness restriction on the discriminator function.

●Spectral normalization: This regularization method normalizes the spectral norm of each layer’s weight matrix in the discriminator (the most significant singular value). This aids in maintaining gradient stability and controlling the discriminator function’s Lipschitz constant.

●Adam optimizer: This adaptive optimization algorithm modifies the learning rate for every parameter based on its prior gradients and moments. The Adam optimizer can assist in handling noisy data, sparse gradients, and various parameter scales.

•3D viewpoint: In 3D objects or settings, GANs frequently find it challenging to comprehend and replicate 3D perspective elements like depth, occlusion, lighting, and shadows. This may lead to flat or distorted visuals that may not correspond to human perception. Furthermore, because GANs must acquire high-level geometric and semantic information in addition to pixel-level characteristics, 3D perspective is a challenging task. The following are a few potential ways to improve the 3D perspective:

●3D-GANs: These GANs use 3D voxel grids rather than 2D pixel grids. Without using intermediate representations or 2D projections, 3D-GANs can produce 3D shapes straight from noise vectors.

●StyleGANs: These GANs use approaches for style transfer to regulate several facets of picture production, including shape, texture, color, and stance. StyleGANs can alter latent codes at various abstraction levels and inject them into various layers of the generating network.

●CycleGANs are GANs that can learn domain-to-domain mappings without paired data. Images from different perspectives, such as front view to side view or aerial view to street view, can be translated using CycleGANs.

Evaluation of GANs: The three main categories of GAN evaluation techniques are quantitative, qualitative, and hybrid. Quantitative approaches use numerical measures to assess the generated samples’ quality, diversity, faithfulness, and similarity. In qualitative approaches, the perceptual realism and diversity of the generated samples are evaluated through human judgments or visual examination. Finally, hybrid techniques combine quantitative and qualitative methods for a more thorough analysis.

The perceptual characteristics of the generated samples are frequently missed by quantitative approaches, which are more objective and scalable than qualitative methods. For instance, some quantitative metrics may prefer fuzzy or noisy samples over sharp and clear ones, or they may need to consider the generated samples’ semantic relevance or coherence. Furthermore, comparing several GAN models and selecting the best one can be challenging because different quantitative indicators cannot agree with one another or with human judgments.

Compared to quantitative approaches, qualitative methods are more empathetic and intuitive but more prone to prejudice and inconsistency. Human judgments, for instance, can differ based on the task, context, assessors’ preferences, and experience level. In addition, conducting qualitative approaches is frequently time-consuming and expensive, particularly for large-scale or high-dimensional data.

By effectively merging quantitative and qualitative methodologies, hybrid methods seek to overcome their respective shortcomings. For instance, some hybrid methods employ quantitative metrics to rank or select samples for qualitative evaluation, while others use quantitative measurements to calibrate or validate quantitative metrics. Compared to quantitative or qualitative methods alone, hybrid methods can offer a more thorough and trustworthy evaluation of GANs.

The design of effective and efficient human-computer interfaces for gathering human feedback, striking a balance between quantitative and qualitative aspects of the evaluation process, and handling potential conflicts or trade-offs between various evaluation criteria are some challenges hybrid methods must overcome.

10.4Other Types of ANNs

Other unique types of ANNs are self-organizing maps (SOMs) and Boltzmann machines (BMs). SOMs, sometimes called Kohonen maps, are a class of unsupervised learning algorithms mainly employed in data visualization and dimensionality reduction applications. They were first used by Teuvo Kohonen in the 1980s, and they worked by discretizing and arranging high-dimensional data into a two-dimensional map while maintaining the original data’s topological characteristics. Boltzmann machines (BMs), on the other hand, are a type of stochastic recurrent neural network that can be used for feature learning, dimensionality reduction, and associative memory. They are named after the Boltzmann distribution in statistical mechanics, which is used in their sampling function.

10.4.1Self-organizing Maps (SOMs)

This unsupervised ML method can provide a low-dimensional representation of a high-dimensional data collection while maintaining the data’s topological structure. It is a method to reduce the data dimensions. So, SOMs can identify patterns and similarities in the data and display them on a two-dimensional map, where each node stands for a collection of related data points. For SOMs to function, a grid of nodes with weight vectors of the same dimension as the input data must first be created. After being randomly initialized, the nodes are iteratively updated based on a competitive learning method. The winner node and its neighboring nodes are chosen for each input data point and are all shifted nearer to the data point. Over time, the neighborhood size and learning rate decrease over time as the nodes converge to stable places.

SOMs can be used for several applications:

•Data visualization: By transforming complex, high-dimensional data sets into a lower-dimensional space, where the distance between nodes shows the similarity between data points, SOMs can aid in the exploration and comprehension of large, complex data sets. SOMs can be used, for instance, to visualize written content and customer segments.

•Data compression: SOMs can shrink the size of big data sets by partitioning them into fewer nodes, each representing a prototype or a cluster centroid. SOMs can be utilized, for instance, to compress images, sounds, or films.

•Finding anomalies: SOMs can locate anomalous data points by calculating their separation from the nearest node or their density on the map. SOMs can be utilized, for instance, to find fraud, network penetration, or disease.

SOMs are of many types, such as:

•U-matrix: This visualization method employs various hues or tones to represent the distance between adjacent nodes on a map. The cluster structure and the boundaries of the data set can be seen in the U-matrix.

•Component planes: This is a method of visualizing weight vectors that display the values of each dimension in distinct maps using various hues or tones. The component planes show the correlations and variances of each attribute in the data set.

•Heat map: This visualization technique uses various colors or tints to indicate how often each node has been chosen as the winner node for the input data points. The distribution and density of the data set can be seen on the hit map.

10.4.2Boltzmann Machines (MBs)

This is a type of ANN that can learn to discover exciting features in data without supervision. They are composed of nodes connected symmetric and bidirectional, meaning that each node can send and receive signals from any other node. Furthermore, the nodes can be visible or hidden, depending on whether they represent observable data or latent variables.

A BM typically consists of several visible and hidden levels, where each visible layer’s nodes are connected to each hidden layer’s nodes. Each node in the hidden layer receives input from the outputs of the visible layer nodes (Fig. 10.20).

Figure 10.20  Boltzmann machine

BMs are stochastic and generative models, meaning they can randomly sample different states of the network based on the probability distribution defined by the connections’ weights and the nodes’ activation function. Learning in BMs aims to adjust the weights so that the network can generate data that resembles the training data.

One of the challenges of BMs is that they are computationally expensive to train, especially when they have many layers of hidden nodes. This is because the learning algorithm requires sampling from the equilibrium distribution of the network, which involves updating all the nodes many times until they reach a stable state. To overcome this problem, a variant called restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM) was proposed, which restricts the connections between nodes such that there are no connections within the same layer (Fig. 10.21).

Figure 10.21  Restricted Boltzmann machine

RBMs can also be stacked together to form deep belief networks (DBNs), which are hierarchical models that can learn multiple levels of abstraction from data. DBNs can be trained layer by layer, using the output of one RBM as the input of another RBM. This way, each RBM can learn features that capture higher-order correlations in the data (Fig. 10.21).

Deep belief networks (DBNs) comprise numerous hidden layers that are connected but not inside the same layer. Each layer functions as a feature extractor, transforming the input data into a higher-level representation.

Pre-training and fine-tuning are the two training steps for DBNs. First, each RBM is pre-trained individually using the contrastive divergence approach, reducing the discrepancy between the data and model distribution. Then, to refine a classification or regression job, the entire DBN is trained collectively using a supervised learning technique, such as gradient descent or backpropagation. DBN applications include speech recognition, picture recognition, natural language processing, and recommendation systems. They can also be enhanced to handle other data kinds, such as continuous, categorical, or temporal data.

Figure 10.21  RBM network as deep belief network (DBN)

10.4.3Modular Neural Networks (MNNs)

MNNs are a type of artificial neural network that consist of multiple modules or subnetworks that perform different tasks or functions (Fig. 10.22). MNNs are designed to overcome some of the limitations of conventional neural networks, such as scalability, complexity, and generalization. MNNs use a divide-and-conquer approach, where a complex problem is decomposed into simpler subproblems that specialized modules can solve. The modules can communicate through various mechanisms, such as shared weights, intermediate outputs, or higher-level representations. The modules can also have different architectures, learning algorithms, and activation functions, depending on the subproblem they are solving.

Figure 10.22  Modular neural network (MNN)

One of the main advantages of MNNs is that they can reduce the computational cost and memory requirements of training and inference, as each module can be trained and updated independently or in parallel. MNNs can also improve the generalization performance and robustness of the network, as each module can learn to focus on specific features or aspects of the input data relevant to its task. Moreover, MNNs can facilitate transferring and reusing knowledge across different domains or tasks, as the modules can be shared or adapted for new problems.

Some types of MNNs are as follows:

•In hierarchical modular neural networks (HMNNs), the modules are arranged in a hierarchical structure, such as a tree or a pyramid (Fig. 10.23). The lower-level modules process the raw input data and extract low-level features. In contrast, the higher-level modules integrate the outputs of the lower-level modules and extract high-level features or make predictions. An example of HMNN is a CNN, where each convolutional layer can be seen as a module that performs feature extraction and pooling.

Figure 10.23  Hierarchical modular neural network (HMNN)

•Cooperative modular neural networks (CMNNs) consist of numerous modules that cooperate to address a common issue.
