12.9.1Risk Assessment and Customer Lifetime Value (CLV)

Risk assessment is the process of evaluating the likelihood and severity of losses that may occur due to various events, such as accidents, natural disasters, illnesses, fraud, etc. ML can help improve risk assessment by using regression, classification, and clustering techniques to analyze historical and real-time data from various sources, such as demographics, credit scores, medical records, social media, etc., and assign risk scores and premiums to customers.

Customer lifetime value (CLV) is the net present value of the future cash flows that a customer generates for a business over their entire relationship. CLV is an important metric for insurance companies, as it helps them optimize their marketing strategies, customer retention, and cross-selling opportunities. ML can help predict CLV by using survival analysis, churn analysis, and recommender systems to estimate how long a customer will stay with the insurer, how likely they are to renew or cancel their policies, and what products or services they are interested in.

However, ML in insurance also faces some challenges and limitations that need to be addressed. For example, ML models require large amounts of high-quality data to train and validate their performance. Therefore, insurers need to ensure that they have proper data governance frameworks and practices in place to ensure data security, compliance, integrity, and availability. Another challenge is that ML models need to be interpretable and explainable to ensure trust and transparency among stakeholders.

One domain where ML can improve customer service is digital insurance. A notable example of a digital insurance company that uses ML is Lemonade. Lemonade offers renters and homeowners insurance through its website and mobile app. Lemonade uses AI-powered chatbots named Maya and Jim to handle customer interactions.

Another domain where ML can enhance claims processing is pay-per-mile car insurance. A leading example of a pay-per-mile car insurance company that uses ML is Metromile. Metromile offers car insurance that charges customers based on how much they drive. Metromile uses telematics devices installed in customers' cars to collect driving data and monitor accidents. When an accident occurs, Metromile's AI claims assistant named Ava analyzes the data and sends a push notification to the customer's smartphone asking them to confirm the details of the incident. Ava then guides the customer through the claims process and arranges for repairs or payments. By using ML, Metromile can automate claims handling, reduce fraud, and provide personalized pricing and coverage.

ML can assist fraud detection in software solutions for insurance. A prominent example of a software company that provides ML solutions for fraud detection in insurance is Shift Technology. Shift Technology uses advanced analytics and machine learning to process large volumes of data from various sources, such as policy documents, claims records, social media, geolocation, etc. By using ML, Shift Technology can help insurance companies identify and prevent fraud, save money, and improve customer loyalty.

Python is a popular programming language that is utilized in many fields, including machine learning (ML). Python has a simple syntax, which makes it easy to analyze and use. 13.3The sklearn Package

Python scikit-learn (sklearn is the newer version) is a widely used and robust ML package that offers a variety of tools and methods for tasks such as data analysis, preprocessing, feature extraction, model selection, assessment, and deployment. It is constructed using NumPy, SciPy, and Matplotlib and seamlessly interfaces with other Python frameworks like pandas and TensorFlow. The objective of scikit-learn is to offer a straightforward and uniform interface for the prevalent ML tasks, including classification, regression, clustering, dimensionality reduction, and anomaly detection. In addition, it provides extensive documentation and abundant examples and tutorials to assist users in getting started and acquiring optimal techniques.

The scikit-learn package offers a significant benefit in the form of high-level abstraction, which conceals the intricacies of the underlying algorithms. This enables users to concentrate on the problem domain and the data without worrying about the complexity. It adheres to the fit–transform–predict principle, wherein most estimators (objects that implement ML algorithms) consist of three primary methods: fit, which trains the model using the provided data; transform, which applies specific data transformations like scaling, encoding, or feature extraction; and predict, which generates predictions on new data using the trained model. This facilitates the concatenation of many estimators into a pipeline, which can then be trained and assessed as a cohesive entity.

The scikit-learn package has the advantage of being compatible with various Python libraries and tools. It is compatible with diverse data types, including NumPy arrays, pandas DataFrames, sparse matrices, and Python dictionaries. It can also connect with other ML frameworks, such as TensorFlow or PyTorch, through wrappers or converters, enabling users to take advantage of the features each platform offers.

The scikit-learn package can perform the following ML tasks:

•Classification: This refers to assigning a specific label to an input based on predetermined criteria. The scikit-learn package offers various classification algorithms, including support vector machines (SVMs), logistic regression, decision trees, and naive Bayes.

•Regression: This refers to using specific characteristics to forecast a continuous value for a given input. The scikit-learn package offers various regression algorithms, including linear regression, ridge regression, and LASSO regression.

•Clustering: This refers to categorizing related inputs using a metric of similarity or distance. The scikit-learn package offers various clustering algorithms, including K-means, hierarchical clustering, and spectral clustering.

•Dimensionality Reduction: This refers to decreasing the number of features or dimensions in the data while retaining as much information as feasible. The scikit-learn package offers various dimensionality reduction algorithms, including principal component analysis (PCA) and non-negative matrix factorization (NMF).

•Model Selection: This involves selecting the optimal model or parameters for a given situation using specific evaluation criteria. The scikit-learn package offers various model selection algorithms, including cross-validation and grid search.

•Preprocessing: This refers to the process of converting the data into a format that is appropriate for ML. The scikit-learn package offers various preprocessing algorithms, including feature scaling, label encoding, and one-hot encoding.

In addition, scikit-learn also provides a range of tools for data analysis, such as data visualization and feature selection. It is designed to be easy to use and efficient, and it has become the most popular ML library for Python.

13.4.1Popular Python Packages

A package is a folder that contains several modules, which are files that contain Python code. A package can also have sub-packages, which are folders inside a package. To use a package, we need to import it or its modules. Some of the most common packages in Python are:

•pandas: This package provides data structures and tools for data analysis. It allows us to manipulate, filter, group, aggregate, and visualize data in tabular or multidimensional formats. It also supports reading and writing data from various sources, such as CSV, Excel, SQL, and JSON.

•NumPy: This package provides numerical computing tools for Python. It allows us to work with arrays, matrices, linear algebra, random numbers, statistics, and more. It also supports broadcasting, vectorization, and integration with other packages, such as pandas and Matplotlib.

•matplotlib.pyplot: This package provides plotting and visualization tools for Python. It allows us to create various types of graphs, such as line plots, bar charts, histograms, scatter plots, and pie charts. It also supports customization of colors, styles, labels, legends, axes, etc.

•sklearn: This package provides ML tools for Python. It allows us to perform tasks such as classification, regression, clustering, dimensionality reduction, feature extraction, model selection, and evaluation. It also supports various algorithms, such as linear models, decision trees, support vector machines, neural networks, etc.

•seaborn: This package provides statistical data visualization tools for Python. It builds on top of matplotlib.pyplot and pandas to create attractive and informative plots. It also supports categorical data analysis, distribution analysis, correlation analysis, regression analysis, etc.

•TensorFlow: This package provides deep learning tools for Python. It allows us to build and train neural networks using tensors, which are multidimensional arrays of data. It also supports various operations, such as activation functions, loss functions, optimizers, metrics, etc. It also supports GPU acceleration and distributed computing.

•IPython: This package provides an interactive shell for Python. It allows us to execute Python code interactively and dynamically. It also supports features such as syntax highlighting, auto-completion, debugging, profiling, magic commands, etc. It also integrates with other packages, such as NumPy and matplotlib.pyplot.

13.4.3Opening Spyder from Anaconda Navigator

Spyder is an integrated development environment (IDE) for Python that comes with Anaconda Navigator. To open the Spyder terminal from Anaconda Navigator, you need to follow these steps:

Figure 13.3  Spyder terminal

A brief explanation of some of the main menus of the Spyder terminal is given below:

•File: This menu allows users to create, open, save, close, print, and run Python files. It also has options to switch projects, restart the kernel, and quit Spyder.

•Edit: This menu lets the user edit the code, such as undo, redo, cut, copy, paste, delete, comment, indent, format, and refactor. It also has options to find and replace text, go to a specific line or definition, and manage bookmarks.

•Source: This menu provides tools to analyze and execute the code, such as code completion, linting, debugging, profiling, testing, and running cells. It also has options to show or hide the outline explorer, the code analysis pane, and the code folding indicators.

•Run: This menu allows the user to run the current file or a selected configuration in different ways, such as in a new dedicated console, in an external system terminal, or with command-line arguments. It also has options to configure the run settings, such as the working directory, the environment variables, and the interpreter.

•Debug: This menu lets users debug the code using breakpoints, conditional breakpoints, watches, and commands. It also has options to show or hide the debugger toolbar and the variable explorer.

•Consoles: This menu provides access to different types of consoles for interactive coding, such as Python consoles, IPython consoles, and system terminals. It also has options to connect to an existing kernel, open a particular console (such as a Qt or Spyder), and manage the console settings.

•Projects: This menu allows users to create, open, close, delete, and import projects. A project is a way of organizing files and settings for a specific task or purpose. It also has options to edit the project properties, such as the name, location, dependencies, and PYTHONPATH.

•Tools: This menu offers various tools and utilities for enhancing the user experience, such as preferences, keyboard shortcuts, online help, an internal console, a dependency manager, a module explorer, and online documentation. It also has options to update Spyder and report issues.

•View: This menu enables the user to customize the appearance and layout of the Spyder terminal. It can show or hide toolbars and panes (such as editor, console, help), zoom in or out of the text size, toggle fullscreen or windowed mode (for macOS), and switch between preset layouts.

•Help: This menu provides access to different sources of information and support for the Spyder terminal. It has options to show the tutorial (for beginners), Spyder documentation (for advanced users), FAQ (for common questions), and the About dialog box (for credits and license).

13.4.4Basic Data Types in Python

Python has five standard data types:

•Number

•String

•List

•Tuple

•Dictionary

Python variables do not need explicit declaration to reserve memory space. The declaration happens automatically when you assign a value to a variable. The equal to (=) sign is used to assign values to variables. The operand to the left of = is the name of the variable and the operand to the right of = is the value stored in the variable.

For example:

>>> var1 = 24

>>> var2 = 28.72

>>> var3 = "Machine Learning"

>>> type(var1)

Out[38]: int

>>> print(var1)

24

>>> type(var2)

Out[39]: float

>>> print(var2)

28.72

>>> type(var3)

Out[40]: str

>>> print(var3)

Machine Learning

Python variables can be easily typecast from one data type to another by using the data type name as a function (actually a wrapper class) and passing the variable to be typecast as a parameter. However, not all data types can be transformed into another; for example, String to Integer/Number is impossible.

>>> var2 = int(var2)

>>> print (var2)

28

>>> type (var2)

Out[42]: int

13.4.5The for and while Loops and the if-else Statement

The for loop

Syntax:

for i in range(<lowerbound>,<upperbound>,<interval>):

    print(i*i)

For example, to print the squares of all integers from 1 to 4.

for i in range(1,5):

    print(i*i)

1

4

9

16

for i in range(1,20,5):

    print(i)

1

6

11

16

The while loop

Syntax:

while < condition>:

    <do something>

For example, to print the cubes of all integers from 1 to 3.

i = 1

while i < 4:

    print(i*i*i)

    i = i + 1

1

8

27

The if-else statement

Syntax:

if < condition>:

    <do something>

else:

      <do something else>

For example, to print the squares of a number if it is negative. If it is a positive number, then print the number.

i = -5

if i < 0:

    print(i*i)

else:

    print(i)

25

13.4.6Writing Functions

Syntax:

def functionname(parametername,…):

    (function_body)

For example, for a function to calculate the factorial of an input number n.

def factorial(n):

    fact = 1

    for i in range(1,n+1):

        fact = fact*i

    return(fact);

k = factorial (4)

13.4.8Using Spyder to Write Python Programs

We will use the Spyder terminal to write all our ML programs. The Spyder terminal (Fig. 13.3) is a tool that allows users to write and run Python programs in an interactive environment. It consists of two main panes: the editor pane and the console pane. The editor pane, located on the left-hand side of the terminal, is where users can write Python code using various features such as syntax highlighting, code completion, and debugging. The console pane, located on the right-hand side of the terminal, is divided into two sub-panes: the plot pane and the I/O pane. The plot pane, located at the top-right corner of the terminal, is where users can see the graphical output of their Python programs, such as charts, graphs, and images. The I/O pane, located at the bottom-right corner of the terminal, is where users can see the terminal output of their Python programs, such as print statements, errors, and warnings. The I/O pane can also be used to enter terminal inputs for the Python programs, such as command-line arguments or user inputs.

13.5Data Operations on the Iris Data Set

The Iris data set is a classic that contains information about three different species of iris flowers: setosa, versicolor, and virginia. Each species has 50 observations of four features: sepal length, sepal width, petal length, and petal width, all measured in centimeters. The statistician Ronald Fisher introduced the data set in 1936 as an example of linear discriminant analysis.

This data set is available from various sources, such as the UCI Machine Learning Repository, Kaggle, scikit-learn, and more. It may have different formats, such as CSV, JSON, pickle, or Python objects, depending on the source.

To download the data set for free, we can use one of the following methods:

•From the UCI Machine Learning Repository: Go to https://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/datasets/Iris and click “Data Folder.” Then download the file “iris.data” which contains the comma-separated values of the data set. Optionally, download the file “iris.names,” which includes the description of the data set.

•From Kaggle: Go to https://www.kaggle.com/uciml/iris and click “Download (4 KB)”. Then unzip the file “iris.zip,” which contains the CSV file “Iris.csv” with the data set.

•From scikit-learn: Use the Python library scikit-learn, which provides a function to load the Iris data set as a Python object. To do this, import the module sklearn and call the function load_iris().

13.5.16Read the Iris Data Set and Combine Sets of Rows

# This line imports the pandas library and gives it the alias pd

import pandas as pd

# This line reads a CSV file named iris.csv and stores it in a variable called data

data = pd.read_csv("iris.csv")

# This line assigns new names to the columns of the data

data.columns = ['Sepal_Length','Sepal_Width','Petal_Length','Petal_Width','Class']

# Create a new variable called data1, which is a subset of the data variable that contains only the first two rows.

data1 = data[0: 2]

display (data1.head)

# Create a new variable called data2 that contains only the rows from index 50 to 51 (inclusive)

data2 = data[50: 52]

display (data2.head)

# Concatenation of the data1 and data2 variables.

data3 = pd.concat ([data1, data2])

display (data3.head)

The program creates a new variable called data1, which is a subset of the data DataFrame that contains only the first two rows. To select a subset of rows from a DataFrame, we can use slicing notation with square brackets. The slicing notation [0:2] means to select the rows from index 0 to index 1 (inclusive), where index is the position of the row in the DataFrame. The index starts from 0 and ends at n - 1, where n is the number of rows in the DataFrame. In this case, n is 150, so the last index is 149. We assign the sliced DataFrame to the variable data1.

The program creates another variable called data2 that contains only the rows from index 50 to 51 (inclusive) from the data DataFrame. To select these rows, we use slicing notation again with [50:52], which means to select the rows from index 50 to index 51 (inclusive). We assign the sliced DataFrame to the variable data2.

The program concatenates or combines the data1 and data2 DataFrames into a new DataFrame called data3. To concatenate DataFrames, we use the pd.concat() function, which takes a list of DataFrames as an argument and returns a new DataFrame with all the rows from each DataFrame in order. # This line imports the pandas library and gives it the alias pd

import pandas as pd

# This line reads a CSV file named iris.csv and stores it in a variable called data

# Use the mean function from numpy to calculate the mean value of the petal length column

# Variance is calculated along the rows (axis=0) rather than along the # columns (axis=1)

We use the display() function to print the output of the following expressions in a formatted way. We use the median() function from NumPy to calculate the median value of the Petal_Length column. The median is the middle value of a sorted list of numbers, or the average of the middle two values if the list has an even number of elements: display (np.median(data[["Petal_Length"]])).

We use the mean() function from NumPy to calculate the mean of the Petal_Length column. The mean is the sum of all values divided by the number of values: display (np.mean(data[["Petal_Length"]])).

We use the var function from NumPy to calculate the variance of the Petal_Length column. The variance is a measure of how spread out the values are from the mean. It is calculated by taking the average of the squared differences between each value and the mean. We use the axis parameter to specify that we want to calculate the variance along the rows (axis=0) rather than along the columns (axis=1): display (np.var(data[["Petal_Length"]], axis= 0)).

13.6Finding Outliers

def find_outlier(ds,col):

quart1 = ds[col].quantile(0.25)

quart3 = ds[col].quantile(0.75)

IQR = quart3 – quart1 #Inter-quartile range

low_val = quart1 – 1.5*IQR

high_val = quart3 + 1.5*IQR

ds = ds.loc[(ds[col] < low_val) | (ds[col] > high_val)]

return ds

We want to write a function to find the outliers in a data set: def find_outlier(ds, col). This function takes a data set (ds) and a column name (col) as input parameters. It returns a subset of the data set that contains only the outlier values in the given column. Outliers are defined as values that are more than 1.5 times the interquartile range (IQR) away from the first or third quartile. The IQR is the difference between the 75th percentile (quart3) and the 25th percentile (quart1) of the column values. The first quartile is calculated by calling the quantile() method on the column with 0.25 as the argument. The third quartile is calculated by calling the quantile() method on the column with 0.75 as the argument. The lower bound for outliers (low_val) is computed by subtracting 1.5 times the IQR from the first quartile. The upper bound for outliers (high_val) is computed by adding 1.5 times the IQR to the third quartile. The loc() method is used to filter the data set by selecting only the rows where the column value is less than low_val or greater than high_val. The filtered data set is returned as the output of the function.

13.7Removing Outliers

def remove_outlier(ds,col):

quart1 = ds[col].quantile(0.25)

quart3 = ds[col].quantile(0.75)

IQR = quart3 – quart1 #Inter-quartile range

low_val = quart1 – 1.5*IQR

high_val = quart3 + 1.5*IQR

df_out = ds.loc[(ds[col] > low_val) & (ds[col] < high_val)]

df_out.dropna(axis=0, how = 'any')

return df_out

The program is a function that takes two arguments: a data set (ds) and a column name (col). The function aims to remove the outliers from the given column of the data set using the interquartile range (IQR) method. The function performs the following steps.

It calculates the first quartile (quart1) and the third quartile (quart3) of the column values using the quantile() method. It computes the IQR as the difference between the third and the first quartiles. It defines the lower and upper bounds for the outliers as 1.5 times the IQR below and above the first and third quartiles, respectively. It filters out the rows of the data set that have column values within the lower and upper bounds using the loc() method and assigns them to a new DataFrame (df_out). It drops any rows that have missing values in any column using the dropna() method. It returns the new DataFrame (df_out) that contains only the non-outlier values of the given column. 13.8Imputing Null Values

def impute_nullvalues(ds,col):

hp_mean = np.mean(data[col])

imputedrows = data[data[col].isnull()]

imputedrows = imputedrows.replace(np.nan, hp_mean)

#Then the portion of the data set not having any missing row is kept apart.

missval_removed_rows = data.dropna(subset=[col])

# Then join back the imputed rows and the remaining part of the data set.

data_mod = pd.concat ([missval_removed_rows, imputedrows])

# data_mod = missval_removed_rows.append(imputedrows, ignore_index=True)

return data_mod

After removing the outliers, we can work on replacing the null values in a column with the mean value of that column using the function, impute_nullvalues(ds, col). This function takes a data set (ds) and a column name (col) as arguments. It returns a modified data set where the missing values in the column are replaced by the mean of the non-missing values.

First, it calculates the mean of the non-missing values in the column using NumPy: hp_mean = np.mean(data[col]). Then, it creates a subset of the data set where the column has missing values using pandas: imputedrows = data[data[col].isnull()]. Next, it replaces the missing values with the mean value using pandas: imputedrows = imputedrows.replace(np.nan, hp_mean). Then, it creates another subset of the data set where the column does not have missing values using pandas: missval_removed_rows = data.dropna(subset=[col]). Finally, it concatenates the two subsets to form the modified data set using pandas: data_mod = pd.concat ([missval_removed_rows, imputedrows]).

Alternatively, it can also use the append() method to join the two subsets: data_mod = missval_removed_rows.append(imputedrows, ignore_index=True). It returns the modified data set as the output of the function: return data_mod.

13.9Capping the Outlier Values

def cap_outlier(ds, col):

outliers = find_outlier(ds,col)

quart1 = data[col].quantile(0.25)

quart3 = data[col].quantile(0.75)

IQR = quart3 – quart1 #Getting the value of IQR

outliers.loc[:, col] = 1.5*IQR # Capping the outlier values with 1.5 times IQR value…

outlier_removed_rows = remove_outlier(data,col)

data_mod = pd.concat ([outlier_removed_rows, outliers])

#data_mod = outlier_removed_rows.append(outliers, ignore_index=True)

return data_mod

This function takes a data set (ds) and a column name (col) as inputs. It returns a modified data set where the outliers in the given column are capped. Capping means replacing the outlier values with a certain threshold value. This can help reduce the effect of outliers on the analysis of the data.

outliers = find_outlier(ds, col)

This line calls another function to find the outliers in the column.

quart1 = data[col].quantile(0.25)

This line calculates the first quartile of the column, which is the median of the lower half of the data.

quart3 = data[col].quantile(0.75)

This line calculates the third quartile of the column, which is the median of the upper half of the data. IQR = quart3 - quart1. This line calculates the interquartile range (IQR), which is the difference between the third and first quartiles.

outliers.loc[:, col] = 1.5*IQR

This line replaces the outlier values with 1.5 times the IQR value, which is a common way to cap outliers.

outlier_removed_rows = remove_outlier(data, col)

This line calls another function to remove the rows that contain outliers from the original data set.

data_mod = pd.concat ([outlier_removed_rows, outliers])

This line concatenates (joins) the data set without outliers and the capped outliers into a new data set.

data_mod = outlier_removed_rows.append(outliers, ignore_index=True)

This line is commented out, which means it is not executed. It is another way to join the two data sets, but it would ignore the original index of the rows. return data_mod. This line returns the modified data set as the output of the function.

13.10Splitting the Data into Training and Testing Data

Splitting the data into training and testing data is a common practice in ML. The main reason for this is to evaluate the performance and generalization ability of the model. The training data fits the model parameters, while the testing data measures how well the model can predict new and unseen data. By splitting the data, we can avoid overfitting, where the model learns too much from the training data and fails to generalize to new data.

The advantages of splitting the data are as follows:

•It allows us to estimate the accuracy and error rate of the model on new data, which is essential for choosing the best model and tuning its hyperparameters.

•It helps us detect and prevent overfitting, leading to poor performance and unreliable predictions.

•It enables us to compare different models and algorithms based on their test results, which can help us to select the most suitable one for our problem.

•It provides us with a way to validate our assumptions and hypotheses about the data and the model, which can improve our understanding and interpretation of the results.

# Splitting the data into Traing and Test data

X_train, X_test, Y_train, Y_test = train_test_split(X_scaled, Y, test_size = 0.2, random_state = 42)

# The parameter, test_size sets the ratio of test data to the input data to 0.2 or 20% and random_state sets

# the seed for random number generator

This program uses the train_test_split() function from the sklearn.model_selection module to split the data into training and testing sets. The function takes four arguments: X_scaled, Y, test_size and random_state. X_scaled is the input data that has been scaled to have zero mean and unit variance. Y is the output data or the target variable. test_size is a float value between 0 and 1 that specifies the proportion of the data to be used as the testing set. In this case, test_size is set to 0.2, which means that 20% of the data will be used for testing and the remaining 80% will be used for training. random_state is an integer value that sets the seed for the random number generator that shuffles the data before splitting. By setting random_state to a fixed value, such as 42, we can ensure that the same split is reproduced every time we run the program. The function returns four values: X_train, X_test, Y_train and Y_test. These are the input and output data for the training and testing sets, respectively.

13.11Training and Evaluating the Model

We must train and evaluate the model in ML to ensure it performs well on new and unseen data. Training the model involves finding the optimal parameters that minimize the loss function on a given training data set. Evaluating the model consists of measuring the model’s performance on a separate validation or testing data set that was not used for training.

The advantages of training and evaluating the model are as follows:

•Training the model allows us to learn from the data and discover the patterns or relationships that can be used for prediction or inference.

•Evaluating the model allows us to assess how well the model generalizes to new data and avoid overfitting or underfitting problems.

•Training and evaluating the model can help us compare different models or algorithms and select the best one for our task or problem.

•Training and evaluating the model can help us improve the model by tuning the hyperparameters, adding regularization, or using more data.

# Training the logistic regression model

model = LogisticRegression()

model.fit(X_train, Y_train)

# making predictions on the test set

Y_pred=model.predict(X_test)

# Evaluating the model performance

from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, confusion_matrix, classification_report

print (accuracy_score(Y_test, Y_pred)) # 1.0

print (confusion_matrix(Y_test, Y_pred)) # [[1 0 0 0] [0 9 0] [0 0 11]]

print (classification_report(Y_test, Y_pred))

The above program is an example of how to use logistic regression to classify data into three classes. The program performs the following steps:

1.It imports the LogisticRegression class from the sklearn.linear_model module and creates an instance of it called model.

2.It uses the fit method of the model to train it on the training data, which consists of two arrays: X_train and Y_train. X_train contains the input features for each sample, and Y_train contains the corresponding class labels (0, 1 or 2).

3.It uses the predict() method of the model to make predictions on the test data, which is another array called X_test. The predictions are stored in an array called Y_pred.

4.It evaluates the model performance by using various metrics from the sklearn.metrics module.

5.It imports the accuracy_score, confusion_matrix, and classification_report functions and prints their results.

The accuracy_score() function returns the fraction of correct predictions, which is 1.0 in this case. The confusion_matrix() function returns a matrix that shows how many samples were correctly or incorrectly classified by each class. The diagonal elements represent the true positives, while the off-diagonal elements represent the false positives and false negatives. The classification_report function returns a text report that summarizes the precision, recall, f1-score and support for each class. Precision is the ratio of true positives to all predicted positives, recall is the ratio of true positives to all actual positives, F1-score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, and support is the number of samples in each class.

13.12Regularization Techniques that Prevent Overfitting

Regularization techniques are methods that modify the learning algorithm or the model to reduce the complexity and prevent overfitting. Regularization techniques can help avoid overfitting by adding constraints or penalties to the model parameters, such as shrinking them towards zero or limiting their magnitude. Some examples of regularization techniques are L1 and L2 regularization, dropout, early stopping, and data augmentation.

Different factors, such as the performance gap between the training and validation sets, the model’s complexity, the data’s size and quality, and the domain knowledge of the problem, can indicate the regularization technique to be used.

Ridge and LASSO are both regularization techniques that help prevent overfitting in linear regression models. Here is a Python program that demonstrates these regularization techniques:

# Import necessary libraries

import numpy as np

import pandas as pd

from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge, Lasso

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error

# Load the dataset

data = pd.read_csv('data.csv')

print(data.shape)

data.head()

# Checking for any null values in dataset

data.isnull().sum()

# Split the dataset into training and testing sets

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(data.drop('target', axis=1), data ['target'], test_size=0.2, random_state=42)

# Ridge Regression

ridge = Ridge(alpha=0.5)

ridge.fit(X_train, y_train)

# Lasso Regression

lasso = Lasso(alpha=0.5)

lasso.fit(X_train, y_train)

# Evaluate the models

ridge_pred = ridge.predict(X_test)

lasso_pred = lasso.predict(X_test)

ridge_mse = mean_squared_error(y_test, ridge_pred)

lasso_mse = mean_squared_error(y_test, lasso_pred)

print("Ridge MSE:", ridge_mse)

print("Lasso MSE:", lasso_mse)

Output:

# Ridge MSE: 0.034

# Lasso MSE: 0.041

In this program, we first import the necessary libraries. Then we load the data set and split it into training and testing sets using the train_test_split function. We then create the ridge and LASSO regression models with the alpha value set to 0.5. We fit these models to the training data and predict the target values for the test set. Finally, we evaluate the models using mean squared error (MSE) and print the results.

The output of the ML program indicates that the ridge regression model has a lower mean squared error (MSE) than the LASSO regression model. This means that the ridge model has a better fit to the data and is less likely to overfit than the lasso model. The ridge model penalizes the coefficients of the features by adding their squared values to the loss function, while the LASSO model penalizes them by adding their absolute values. The LASSO model can shrink some coefficients to zero, resulting in feature selection, but it can also introduce bias and variance. The ridge model preserves all the features, but it can also reduce their impact on the prediction. Therefore, the choice of the regularization parameter (alpha) is crucial for both models, as it determines the trade-off between bias and variance. A cross-validation technique can be used to find the optimal alpha value that minimizes the MSE for both models.

13.13Implement Linear Regression

Here is a complete Python program that implements linear regression:

# Import necessary libraries

import numpy as np

import pandas as pd

from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Load dataset

data = pd.read_csv("Salary_Data.csv")

# Exploring dataset

data.head()

data.shape

# Checking for any Null values in the imported Datasets

data.isnull().sum()

# Split data into features and target

X = data.iloc[:,:-1].values

y = data.iloc[:, -1].values

# Create Linear Regression model

model = LinearRegression()

# Fit the model to the data

model.fit(X,y)

# Predict new values

new_data = np.array([[5], [10], [15]])

predictions = model.predict(new_data)

# Print the predictions

print(predictions)

# Plot dataset

plt.scatter(X, y, color= 'blue')

plt.plot(X, model.predict(X), color='red')

plt.title('SALARY VS EXPERIENCE (training set)')

plt.xlabel('Experience in Years')

plt.ylabel('Salary in Rupees')

plt. show()

The program follows these steps:

1.Import the necessary libraries: The program imports NumPy, pandas, sklearn, and Matplotlib as they provide useful functions and methods for data manipulation, analysis, modeling, and visualization.

2.Load the data set: The program reads data from Salary_Data.csv and stores it in a pandas DataFrame called data.

3.Exploring the data set: The program uses the head() and shape() methods to display the first five rows and the dimensions of the data, respectively.

4.Checking for any null values in the imported data sets: The program uses the isnull() and sum() methods to count the number of missing values in each column of the data.

5.Split data into features and target: The program uses the iloc() method to select the first column as the feature variable X (experience) and the second column as the target variable y (salary).

6.Create a linear regression model: The program creates an instance of the LinearRegression class from sklearn.linear_model module and assigns it to a variable called model.

7.Fit the model to the data: The program uses the fit() method to train the model on the feature and target variables.

13.18Implement Steepest Descent

# Python implementation of Steepest Descent algorithm

# Import required libraries

import numpy as np

from scipy import optimize

# Define the objective function

def objective(x):

    return (x[0]**2 + x[1]**2)

# Define the gradient of the objective function

def gradient(x):

    return np.array([2*x[0], 2*x[1]])

# Define the steepest descent algorithm

def steepest_descent(x0, objective, gradient, max_iter=100, tol=1e-6):

  

    # Define initial values

    x = x0

    iter_count = 0

  

    # Iterate until convergence

    while iter_count < max_iter:

        # Compute the gradient at the current point

        grad = gradient(x)

        # Compute the step size using line search

        alpha = optimize.line_search(objective, gradient, x, -grad)[0]

         # Compute the new point by taking a step in the direction of the negative gradient

        x_new = x - alpha*grad

      

        # Check for convergence

        if np.linalg.norm(x_new - x) < tol:

            break

      

        # Update the point and iteration count

        x = x_new

        iter_count += 1

  

    # Return the solution and number of iterations

    return x, iter_count

# Define the initial point

x0 = np.array([1, 2])

# Run the steepest descent algorithm

x_opt, iter_count = steepest_descent(x0, objective, gradient)

# Print the results

print('Optimal solution:', x_opt)

print('Number of iterations:', iter_count)

The above program is an implementation of the steepest descent algorithm, which is a method for finding a local minimum of a differentiable function. The program consists of the following steps:

1.It imports the NumPy library for numerical computations and the SciPy library for optimization tools.

2.It defines the objective function that needs to be minimized. In this case, it is a simple quadratic function of two variables: f (x) = x[0]**2 + x[1]**2. The objective function takes a NumPy array as input and returns a scalar value as output.

3.It defines the gradient of the objective function, which is a vector that points in the direction of the steepest ascent of the function. The gradient is computed by taking the partial derivatives of the objective function with respect to each variable: grad(x) = [2*x[0], 2*x[1]]. The gradient function also takes a NumPy array as input and returns a NumPy array as output.

4.It defines the steepest descent algorithm, which is a function that takes four arguments: x0 (the initial point), objective (the objective function), gradient (the gradient function), and optionally max_iter (the maximum number of iterations) and tol (the tolerance for convergence). The algorithm works as follows. It initializes the current point to x0 and sets the iteration count to zero. It repeats the following steps until either the iteration count reaches max_iter or the change in the point is less than tol. It evaluates the gradient at the current point and stores it in a variable called grad. It uses the line search function from SciPy to find an optimal step size that minimizes the objective function along the direction of the negative gradient. The line search function returns a scalar value called alpha. It updates the current point by subtracting alpha times grad from it. This moves the point closer to a local minimum of the objective function. It increments the iteration count by one. It returns the final point and the number of iterations as a tuple.

5.It defines an initial point to start from. In this case, it is a NumPy array with values [1, 2].

6.It calls the steepest descent algorithm with the initial point, objective function, and gradient function as arguments. It stores the returned values in two variables: x_opt (the optimal solution) and iter_count (the number of iterations).

7.It prints out the optimal solution and number of iterations to show the results.

               'max_features': max_features,

               'max_depth': max_depth,

               'min_samples_split': min_samples_split,

               'min_samples_leaf': min_samples_leaf,

               'bootstrap': bootstrap}

# Apply randomized search to find the best hyperparameters

# Print the best hyperparameters

13.22Implement Single-Layer Perceptron Learning Algorithm

Here’s a Python program to implement the single-layer perceptron learning algorithm:

# Importing necessary libraries

import numpy as np

# Defining the single layer perceptron learning algorithm function

def perceptron_learning(training_data, targets, learning_rate, epochs):

    # Initializing the weights and bias

    weights = np.zeros(training_data.shape[1])

    bias = 0.0

    # Iterating for the given number of epochs

    for i in range(epochs):

        # Iterating over the training data

        for j, x in enumerate(training_data):

            # Calculating the predicted output

            y_predicted = np.dot(weights, x) + bias

            # Updating the weights and bias based on the error

            if targets[j]*y_predicted <= 0:

                weights += learning_rate * targets[j] * x

                bias += learning_rate * targets[j]

    # Returning the learned weights and bias

    return weights, bias

# Testing the function with sample data

training_data = np.array([[0, 0], [0, 1], [1, 0], [1, 1]])

targets = np.array([-1, -1, -1, 1])

learning_rate = 0.1

epochs = 10

weights, bias = perceptron_learning(training_data, targets, learning_rate, epochs)

print("Learned weights:", weights)

print("Learned bias:", bias)

Output:

Learned weights: [0.2 0.1]

Learned bias: -0.20000000000000004

In this program, we first import the NumPy library, which is used for mathematical operations. We then define a function called perceptron_learning(), which takes in the training data, targets, learning rate, and number of epochs as inputs. Inside the function, we initialize the weights and bias to zero and iterate over the training data for the given number of epochs. For each iteration, we calculate the predicted output, update the weights and bias based on the error, and continue until convergence. Finally, we return the learned weights and bias.

To test the function, we use sample data consisting of four input vectors and their corresponding target outputs. We set the learning rate and number of epochs to 0.1 and 10, respectively. We then call the perceptron_learning() function with the sample data and print the learned weights and bias.

13.23Implement Radial Basis Functions

Here’s a sample Python code to implement radial basis functions:

import numpy as np

# Define the radial basis function

def rbf(x, c, s):

    return np.exp(-1 / (2 * s**2) * (x-c)**2)

# Generate sample data

x = np.linspace(-5, 5, 100)

y = np.sin(x)

# Define the centers and standard deviation of the radial basis functions

centers = np.linspace(-5, 5, 9)

sigma = 0.5

# Create the design matrix

X = np.zeros((len(x), len(centers)))

for i in range(len(x)):

    for j in range(len(centers)):

        X[i,j] = rbf(x[i], centers[j], sigma)

# Solve for the weights

w = np.linalg.solve(np.dot(X.T, X), np.dot(X.T, y))

# Predict using the model

y_pred = np.dot(X, w)

# Plot the results

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.plot(x, y, label='True function')

plt.plot(x, y_pred, label='Predicted function')

plt.legend()

plt.show()

Output:

This code defines the radial basis function (RBF) as a Gaussian function with a center c and standard deviation s. It then generates sample data x and y and defines the centers and standard deviation of the RBFs. The design matrix X is created by applying the RBF to each data point and center, and the weights w are solved for using linear regression. Finally, the model is used to predict y_pred and plot the results.

13.28Implement Locality Preserving Projection

Locality preserving projection (LPP) is a dimensionality reduction technique that is used to reduce the number of features in a data set by preserving the local structure of the data. It is implemented in Python using the scikit-learn library.

Here is a Python program for LPP with explanations and comments:

import numpy as np

from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors

def LPP(X, n_components):

  

    Locality Preserving Projection (LPP)

  

    Parameters:

    X (array-like, shape (n_samples, n_features)): Input data.

    n_components (int): Desired dimensionality of output data.

  

    Returns:

    X_lpp (array-like, shape (n_samples, n_components)): Projected data.

  

    # Step 1: Compute the affinity matrix W

    n_samples, n_features = X.shape

    knn = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=n_samples, algorithm='auto').fit(X)

    _, indices = knn.kneighbors(X)

    W = np.zeros((n_samples, n_samples))

    for i in range(n_samples):

        xi = X[i]

        xi_neighbors = X[indices[i]][1:]

        for j in range(n_samples):

            xj = X[j]

            xj_neighbors = X[indices[j]][1:]

            if j in indices[i]:

                W[i, j] = 1

            elif j in indices[indices[i]]:

                W[i, j] = 0.5 / (np.linalg.norm(xi - xj) ** 2)

            else:

                W[i, j] = 0

  

    # Step 2: Compute the graph Laplacian L

    D = np.diag(W.sum(axis=1))

    L = D - W

  

    # Step 3: Compute the eigenvectors of L

    eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eig(L)

  

    # Step 4: Choose the eigenvectors corresponding to the n_components smallest eigenvalues

    indices = np.argsort(eigenvalues)[:n_components]

    X_lpp = eigenvectors[:, indices].real

        return X_lpp

The LPP function takes in an input data array of shape (n_samples, n_features) and a desired output dimensionality, n_components. It returns the projected data array X_lpp of shape (n_samples, n_components). The LPP algorithm consists of four steps:

1.Compute the affinity matrix W: For each sample xi in X, find its n_samples nearest neighbors in X using sklearn.neighbors.NearestNeighbors. For each pair of samples xi and xj, compute their affinity weight W[i, j] as follows:

•If xj is one of xi’s nearest neighbors, set W[i, j] = 1.

•If xj is one of the nearest neighbors of one of xi’s nearest neighbors (xj is a second-order neighbor of xi), set W[i, j] = 0.5 / ||xi - xj||^2, where ||.|| denotes the Euclidean distance.

•Otherwise, set W[i, j] = 0.

2.Compute the graph Laplacian L: Compute the diagonal matrix D whose i-th diagonal element is the sum of the i-th row of W. Compute L = D - W.

3.Compute the eigenvectors of L: Compute the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of L.

4.Choose the eigenvectors corresponding to the n_components smallest eigenvalues: Sort the eigenvalues in ascending order and choose the eigenvectors corresponding to the n_components smallest eigenvalues. Return the matrix whose columns are these eigenvectors as X_lpp.

13.29Implement Logic Gates without Perceptron Model

# Logic gate program

def and_gate(input1, input2):

        return 1

    else:

        return 0

# Define the OR gate function

def or_gate(input1, input2):

    if input1 == 0 and input2 == 0:

        return 0

    else:

        return 1

# Define the NOR gate function

def nor_gate(input1, input2):

    if input1 == 0 and input2 == 0:

        return 1

    else:

        return 0

# Define the XOR gate function

def xor_gate(input1, input2):

    if input1 != input2:

        return 1

    else:

        return 0

# Test the logic gate functions

print("AND gate:")

print(and_gate(0,1)) # Output: 0

print(and_gate(1,0)) # Output: 0

print(and_gate(1,1)) # Output: 1

print(or_gate(0,1)) # Output: 1

print(or_gate(1,0)) # Output: 1

print(or_gate(1,1)) # Output: 1

print("NOR gate:")

print(nor_gate(0,0)) # Output: 1

print(nor_gate(0,1)) # Output: 0

print(nor_gate(1,0)) # Output: 0

13.30Implement Logic Gates with Perceptron Model

Python implementations of logic gates (AND/OR/NOR/XOR) using perceptron-based methods can be achieved using a combination of linear algebra and activation functions. The perceptron-based methods use a linear combination of inputs and weights to produce an output. The output is then passed through an activation function to produce the desired output. XOR cannot be implemented using a single-layer perceptron because it is a non-linear function. XOR requires two layers of perceptrons to produce the desired output. The first layer is used to produce the linear combination of inputs and weights, and the second layer to produce the non-linear output.

To implement an AND gate using perceptron-based methods, we can assign weights and biases to the inputs in such a way that the perceptron produces a positive output only if both inputs are positive. For example, we can set the weights to 1 and the bias to -1.5. This ensures that the output is positive only if both inputs are positive.

Here is a Python program for implementing an AND gate using perceptron-based methods:

def perceptron_AND(x1, x2):

    w1, w2, bias = 1, 1, -1.5

    output = x1*w1 + x2*w2 + bias

    if output > 0:

        return 1

    else:

        return 0

# Example usage

print(perceptron_AND(0, 0)) # Output: 0

print(perceptron_AND(0, 1)) # Output: 0

print(perceptron_AND(1, 0)) # Output: 0

print(perceptron_AND(1, 1)) # Output: 1

Here is a Python program for implementing an OR gate using perceptron-based methods:

def perceptron_OR(x1, x2):

    w1, w2, bias = 1, 1, -0.5

    output = x1*w1 + x2*w2 + bias

    if output > 0:

        return 1

    else:

        return 0

# Example usage

print(perceptron_OR(0, 0)) # Output: 0

print(perceptron_OR(0, 1)) # Output: 1

print(perceptron_OR(1, 0)) # Output: 1

print(perceptron_OR(1, 1)) # Output: 1

To implement a NOR gate, we can simply invert the output of the OR gate using the NOT operator. For example:

def perceptron_NOR(x1, x2):

    return not perceptron_OR(x1, x2)

# Example usage

print(perceptron_NOR(0, 0)) # Output: 1

print(perceptron_NOR(0, 1)) # Output: 0

print(perceptron_NOR(1, 0)) # Output: 0

print(perceptron_NOR(1, 1)) # Output: 0

Finally, to implement an XOR gate using perceptron-based methods, we need to use multiple perceptrons. One way to do this is to use two perceptrons to implement the AND and OR functions, and then combine their outputs using another perceptron.

Here is a Python program for implementing an XOR gate using perceptron-based methods:

def perceptron_XOR(x1, x2):

    and_output = perceptron_AND(x1, x2)

    or_output = perceptron_OR(x1, x2)

    return perceptron_AND(not and_output, or_output)

# Example usage

print(perceptron_XOR(0, 0)) # Output: 0

print(perceptron_XOR(0, 1)) # Output: 1

print(perceptron_XOR(1, 0)) # Output: 1

print(perceptron_XOR(1, 1)) # Output: 0

# Load the MNIST data set

(x_train, y_train), (x_test, y_test) = keras.datasets.mnist.load_data()

# Preprocess the data

x_train = x_train.astype("float32") / 255

x_test = x_test.astype("float32") / 255

x_train = x_train.reshape((x_train.shape[0], 28, 28, 1))

x_test = x_test.reshape((x_test.shape[0], 28, 28, 1))

y_train = keras.utils.to_categorical(y_train, 10)

y_test = keras.utils.to_categorical(y_test, 10)

# Define the CNN model

model = keras.Sequential(

    [

        layers.Conv2D(32, (3, 3), activation="relu", input_shape=(28, 28, 1)),

        layers.MaxPooling2D(pool_size=(2, 2)),

        layers.Conv2D(64, (3, 3), activation="relu"),

        layers.MaxPooling2D(pool_size=(2, 2)),

        layers.Flatten(),

        layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax"),

    ]

)

# Compile the model

model.compile(loss="categorical_crossentropy", optimizer="adam", metrics=["accuracy"])

# Train the model

model.fit(x_train, y_train, epochs=5, batch_size=64, validation_split=0.1)

# Evaluate the model on the test set

test_loss, test_acc = model.evaluate(x_test, y_test)

print(f"Test accuracy: {test_acc}")

13.32Introduction to R Programming

R is a programming language and free software developed by Ross Ihaka and Robert Gentleman in 1993 at the University of Auckland, New Zealand. R is an implementation of the S programming language, which was created by John Chambers and others at Bell Labs in the 1970s. R also incorporates features from other languages, such as lexical scoping from Scheme. R is widely used for statistical computing and graphics, as well as data analysis and ML.

R can be installed on various operating systems, such as Windows, Linux, and Mac OS X. The official website of R provides instructions and links for downloading and installing the latest version. Alternatively, R can be used online through web-based platforms, such as RStudio Cloud, which allows users to create, share, and collaborate on R projects in the browser.

R is useful for ML because it offers a large collection of packages that implement various algorithms and techniques for data mining, classification, clustering, regression, neural networks, deep learning, and more. R also provides tools for data manipulation, visualization, and reporting, which are essential for exploring and communicating the results of machine learning models.

R is a versatile and powerful language that can handle complex and large-scale data analysis problems. It also has a vibrant and active community of users and developers who contribute to its development and improvement. R is one of the most popular languages for data science and ML in the world.

13.32.1Installing R

To install R on Windows, you need to follow these steps:

1.Go to the CRAN website (https://cran.r-project.org/) and click on the “Download R for Windows” link.

2.Click on the “Install R for the first time” link to download the R executable file (R-4.3.1-win.exe).

3.Run the R executable file and allow the app to make changes to your device. Select the installation language and follow the installation instructions.

4.After the installation is complete, you can launch R by clicking on the R icon on your desktop or Start menu.

To test that the installation is working, you can try some simple commands in the R console, such as:

print("Hello, world!") - to print a message.

2 + 2 - to perform arithmetic operations.

sessionInfo() - to check the version and details of your R session.

13.32.2Installing RStudio

If you want to use a more user-friendly interface for writing and executing R code, you can also install RStudio, which is an integrated development environment (IDE) for R. To install RStudio, you need to follow these steps:

1.Go to the RStudio website (https://rstudio.com/) and click on the Download button.

2.Choose the free version of RStudio Desktop for Windows and click on the Download button.

3.Run the RStudio executable file (RStudio-X.X.X.exe) and follow the installation instructions.

4.After the installation is complete, you can launch RStudio by clicking on the RStudio icon on your desktop or Start menu.

To test that RStudio is working, you can create a new R script file by clicking on the File menu and selecting New File and then R Script. You can write some R code in the script editor and run it by clicking on the Run button or by pressing Ctrl+Enter. You should view the output of your code in the console.

You have now successfully installed R and RStudio on your Windows operating system and tested that they are working.

RStudio can also be used directly from Anaconda Navigator (see Section 13.1):

1.Launch Anaconda Navigator from the Start menu (Windows) or the Applications folder (MacOS)

2.Click on the Environments tab on the left side of the Navigator window.

3.Click on the Create button at the bottom of the window and give a name to your new environment (such as R_env)

4.In the list of packages, select R and click on Apply.

5.Wait for the installation to complete and then click on the Home tab.

6.In the list of applications, select RStudio and click on Install.
